questions.a: Children's Social Security numbers are targeted because misuse may go unnoticed for years; a freeze blocks new accounts. Parents can request freezes for children under 16.

questions.q: Does a freeze affect your credit score?
questions.a: No.

days.guide: Research FCRA and California consumer rights; draft a CFPB or DFPI complaint for a sample problem.

questions.q: What right does the FCRA give you?
questions.a: To see your credit report and dispute inaccurate information, which must be investigated, usually within 30 days.

days.guide: The student makes the scam-prevention guide and takes the quiz.

questions.q: What should you do if a 'bank' calls asking for a code sent to your phone?
questions.a: Hang up — never share the code; call the bank using the number on your card.

weeks.prep: Gather rental listings near a chosen college or job, a sample California lease, and CA Courts Self-Help tenant pages. Know current rules: since July 1, 2024 (AB 12), most landlords may charge a security deposit of no more than one month's rent (small landlords owning no more than two properties with four total units may charge up to two months); deposits must be returned with an itemized statement within 21 days after move-out. Prepare or assign the NGPF post-assessment/semester final.
misconceptions: Applying the 30% rule to gross vs. net pay inconsistently. The 30% guideline usually uses gross income; on net pay rent at 30% is even tighter.
Forgetting move-in costs. First month's rent, security deposit, application fees, utilities setup and furniture add up quickly.
Signing a lease without reading it. Note late fees, repair responsibilities, guest rules, and termination terms.
weeks.assessment_key: Semester final: score with the NGPF post-assessment key (target 80%+). Capstone budget rubric: 4 = realistic net pay from a researched job; rent at or near 30% of gross income (or with roommates); utilities, food, transportation, insurance (health, renters, auto), phone, savings (emergency fund and retirement), debt payments; balanced; brief presentation answering parent questions; 3 = minor omissions; 2 = unrealistic or unbalanced; 1 = incomplete. Rental check example: gross pay $3,000/month → 30% rule max rent $900; move-in for $1,200 rent with one-month deposit = $1,200 + $1,200 = $2,400 plus fees.

days.guide: Find three rentals, apply the 30% rule and compute move-in costs.

questions.q: Gross monthly income $2,800. Max rent under the 30% rule?
Rent $1,100, deposit one month, $50 application fee. Move-in cost?

days.guide: Annotate a sample California lease for rent, deposit, late fees, repairs, termination; list tenant rights and the 21-day deposit return rule.

questions.q: How long does a California landlord have to return a security deposit?
questions.a: 21 days after move-out, with an itemized statement of any deductions.

questions.q: What is the maximum security deposit for most California rentals?
questions.a: One month's rent (since July 1, 2024), with an exception allowing two months for certain small landlords.

days.guide: Write a roommate agreement: rent split, utilities, guests, chores, quiet hours, what happens if someone moves out.

questions.q: Why put a roommate agreement in writing?
questions.a: It sets clear expectations and gives a reference if disagreements arise.

days.guide: Build the complete first-year independent life budget.

questions.q: What categories must the life budget include?
questions.a: Net pay, rent, utilities, food, transportation, insurance, phone, savings, debt payments and some fun money.

days.guide: Give the semester final and have the student present the capstone budget.

questions.q: What is one change you'd make to your budget if rent rose by $150?
questions.a: Answers vary; e.g. find a roommate, cut wants, or increase income.

weeks.prep: Make sure the student's CaliforniaColleges.edu account works; open the O*NET Interest Profiler (mynextmove.org) and the BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook. Help line up a professional for a 20-minute informational interview (in person, phone or video).
misconceptions: Treating an interest inventory as a verdict. It suggests areas to explore; it doesn't decide a career.
Choosing a career by salary alone. Consider interests, values, training time and cost, working conditions and job outlook.
Asking for a job in an informational interview. The purpose is to learn; asking for advice and referrals is fine, asking for a job is not.
weeks.assessment_key: Career exploration report rubric (two pages, 4 levels): 4 = summarizes both interest inventory results (e.g. Holland/RIASEC codes) and how they compare; five strengths with evidence; values ranking; three researched careers with duties, education, median pay, outlook and California openings with sources; key takeaways from the informational interview; a SMART five-year goal; 3 = complete with thin evidence; 2 = missing a section; 1 = incomplete.

days.guide: Take the CaliforniaColleges.edu career assessment and the O*NET Interest Profiler; compare results.

questions.q: What are the six RIASEC interest areas used by O*NET?
questions.a: Realistic, Investigative, Artistic, Social, Enterprising, Conventional.

days.guide: Rank work values (pay, security, creativity, helping others, independence, work-life balance) and list five strengths with evidence.

questions.q: Why give evidence for a strength?
questions.a: Employers and colleges believe examples (a project you led, a skill you used) more than claims.

days.guide: Research three careers in the OOH: duties, education, pay, outlook, California openings.

questions.q: What does 'job outlook' mean in the OOH?
questions.a: The projected percent change in employment over the next ten years compared with the average for all occupations.

days.guide: Prepare 10 questions and conduct the informational interview; send a thank-you.

questions.q: Give two good informational interview questions.
questions.a: 'What does a typical day look like?' and 'What do you wish you'd known before entering this field?' (also: how did you get started, what skills matter most).

days.guide: The student writes the career exploration report; score with the rubric.

questions.q: Make 'have a good career' a SMART five-year goal.
questions.a: Example: 'By June 2031, complete an AS in Nursing and pass the NCLEX-RN to work as a registered nurse in Sacramento.'

weeks.prep: Open CaliforniaColleges.edu college search, College Scorecard (collegescorecard.ed.gov), and three colleges' net price calculators. Have family income information available for the calculators (estimates are fine).
misconceptions: Judging colleges by sticker price. Net price (cost after grants and scholarships) can make a private school cheaper than a public one for some families.
Applying only to reach schools. A balanced list has likely, match and reach options, including at least one affordable likely option.
Thinking a 4-year college is the only path. Community college, apprenticeships, CTE certificates and the military lead to good careers.
weeks.assessment_key: Balanced list rubric: 4 = eight or more options with a mix of likely, match and reach (and/or apprenticeship/CTE/military), each with graduation rate, median debt and median earnings from College Scorecard, net price estimates for three schools, and a rationale connecting to career goals; 3 = balanced but missing some data; 2 = unbalanced or missing data; 1 = incomplete. Systems chart key: UC — 10 campuses (9 enroll undergraduates), research universities, most selective, higher tuition; CSU — 23 campuses, teaching and career-focused, moderate tuition; California Community Colleges — 116 colleges, open access, lowest cost, certificates, associate degrees and transfer; private colleges — varied missions and cost, often significant institutional aid.

days.guide: Make a chart comparing UC, CSU, California Community Colleges and private colleges by mission, cost, size and admission.

questions.q: How many campuses do the UC, CSU and California Community College systems have?
questions.a: UC: 10 campuses (9 with undergraduates); CSU: 23; Community Colleges: 116.

questions.q: What are UC and CSU's basic subject requirements called?
questions.a: The a–g requirements (15 year-long college-prep courses).

days.guide: Research a California registered apprenticeship, a CTE certificate and military enlistment requirements.

questions.q: What is a registered apprenticeship?
questions.a: A paid job with structured on-the-job training plus classroom instruction, leading to a nationally recognized credential (e.g. electrician, plumber).

days.guide: Find eight schools on CaliforniaColleges.edu and College Scorecard; record graduation rate, median debt and earnings.

questions.q: What does College Scorecard's 'median earnings' show?
questions.a: The typical earnings of former students several years after entering the school.

days.guide: Run three net price calculators with your family.

questions.q: What is net price?
questions.a: Cost of attendance minus grants and scholarships — what the family actually pays (through savings, income, work or loans).

days.guide: The student submits the balanced list with a rationale.

questions.q: What's an 'impacted' major?
questions.a: A major with more qualified applicants than space, so it has higher admission standards.

weeks.prep: Read the UC 'Homeschooled students' admissions page and the CSU homeschool guidance (check the current wording; requirements change, and UC no longer uses SAT/ACT scores in admission). Gather the student's records: courses, texts used, grades, AP/test scores, college classes.
misconceptions: Assuming homeschool courses automatically count as a–g. UC/CSU have specific ways for homeschoolers to show a–g (e.g. UC-approved online courses, AP exams, transferable college courses); check the current options on each system's page.
Vague course descriptions. Admissions readers need texts, topics, labs, assessments and how grades were determined.
Inflated or inconsistent grades. The transcript, descriptions and test scores should tell a consistent story.
weeks.assessment_key: Draft four-year course list and descriptions rubric: 4 = every course listed by year with subject, a–g letter where applicable, grade, and semester credits (10 per year-long course); at least the a–g minimums (2 years history, 4 English, 3 math, 2 lab science, 2 language other than English, 1 visual/performing arts, 1 elective); three course descriptions each naming the curriculum and texts, major topics, labs/projects, assessments and grading method; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = missing a–g mapping or descriptions thin; 1 = incomplete.

days.guide: Read UC's homeschool page and summarize how a–g can be met.

questions.q: Name two ways a homeschooled student can demonstrate a–g subject work for UC.
questions.a: Examples: courses from UC-approved a–g online providers, qualifying AP exam scores, and UC-transferable community college courses (check UC's current page for all options).

days.guide: Read CSU's homeschool guidance; list required documents and how to report courses in Cal State Apply.

questions.q: What does Cal State Apply ask applicants to enter?
questions.a: A self-reported academic record of courses and grades, plus test scores (if any), activities and personal information.

days.guide: Build the four-year course list with a–g letters, grades and credits.

questions.q: List the a–g subject areas and minimum years.
questions.a: a) history 2, b) English 4, c) math 3, d) lab science 2, e) language other than English 2, f) visual and performing arts 1, g) college-prep elective 1.

days.guide: Write three course descriptions for the counselor packet.

questions.q: What should a course description include?
questions.a: Course title, level, curriculum/texts, topics covered, labs or projects, assessments and how the grade was determined.

days.guide: Parent reviews the list and descriptions for accuracy.

questions.q: Why must the course list match the transcript exactly?
questions.a: Discrepancies between self-reported records and the final transcript can cause admission offers to be withdrawn.

weeks.prep: Have the transcript draft, UC Application and Cal State Apply logins (or practice access). Check current application fees and fee-waiver rules (each system grants waivers for up to four campuses to eligible students).
misconceptions: Estimating grades from memory. Enter the self-reported record exactly from the transcript.
Listing activities without impact. Use specific numbers and results ('tutored 6 children weekly for 2 years').
Missing confirmation. Save confirmation numbers and portal logins; check email and portals regularly.
weeks.assessment_key: Application audit checklist: [ ] personal info matches legal documents; [ ] every course and grade matches the transcript; [ ] a–g categories correct; [ ] up to 20 activities/awards, each ≤ 350 characters, specific and quantified; [ ] PIQs (UC) complete; [ ] fee or fee waiver; [ ] submitted with confirmation numbers logged; [ ] portal logins saved; [ ] consistent names/dates across applications. Pass = all checked or documented plan for a future cycle.

days.guide: Tour each section of the UC Application and Cal State Apply; note required information and fee-waiver eligibility.

questions.q: How many UC campuses can an eligible student apply to with a fee waiver?
questions.a: Up to four.

questions.q: What sections does the UC Application include?
questions.a: Personal information, academic history, test scores (optional/if applicable), activities and awards, Personal Insight Questions, and review/submit.

days.guide: Enter or practice entering the self-reported academic record exactly from the transcript.

questions.q: Why is the UC academic record called 'self-reported'?
questions.a: Applicants enter their own courses and grades; transcripts are verified later if admitted.

days.guide: Write up to 20 activity entries with concise, quantified descriptions (350 characters).

questions.q: Improve: 'Volunteered at food bank.'
questions.a: 'Sorted and packed 400+ lbs of food weekly at the Sacramento Food Bank; trained 5 new volunteers (2023–present, 4 hrs/week).'

days.guide: Verify submissions (or a future cycle plan) and log confirmation numbers and logins.

questions.q: After submitting, what should you watch for?
questions.a: Emails and portal messages requesting documents, portal setup for each campus, and deadlines.

days.guide: Parent or peer audits the application with the checklist.

questions.q: Why check consistency across applications?
questions.a: Inconsistencies in names, grades or dates can raise questions or delay processing.

weeks.prep: Print the eight UC Personal Insight Questions and UC's PIQ guide (admission.universityofcalifornia.edu). Students answer four, up to 350 words each.
misconceptions: Writing a résumé in paragraph form. PIQs need a specific example and reflection on what it shows about you.
Trying to sound impressive instead of genuine. Simple, honest language and real detail work best.
Ignoring the question asked. Each PIQ should clearly answer its prompt.
weeks.assessment_key: PIQ rubric (each of four, 4 levels): 4 = directly answers the prompt; one focused, specific example (who, what, when, actions taken); reflection on what the student learned or how they grew; shows qualities not visible elsewhere in the application; clear, active, error-free writing; ≤ 350 words; 3 = specific but reflection thin; 2 = general claims, few details; 1 = off-topic or over the limit. Reflection paragraph: proficient answers name what each PIQ shows readers (e.g. leadership, curiosity, resilience).

days.guide: Read all eight prompts and UC's guide; brainstorm two stories for each; pick four.

questions.q: How many PIQs must you answer, and what's the word limit?
questions.a: Four of the eight, up to 350 words each.

questions.q: Which prompt fits writing about homeschooling as an educational experience?
questions.a: Prompt 4 (taking advantage of an educational opportunity or overcoming an educational barrier).

days.guide: Draft two PIQs with specific examples and reflection.

questions.q: What's the difference between telling and showing in a PIQ?
questions.a: Telling: 'I am a leader.' Showing: a specific story of what you did as a leader and the result.

days.guide: Draft the remaining two PIQs.

questions.q: What two parts should each PIQ include?
questions.a: A specific example (what happened and what you did) and reflection (what it shows or how you grew).

days.guide: Revise for specificity, active voice and word count after reading aloud.

questions.q: Rewrite in active voice: 'The fundraiser was organized by me.'
questions.a: 'I organized the fundraiser.'

days.guide: Submit four polished PIQs with a reflection; score with the rubric.

questions.q: Why avoid repeating your activities list in PIQs?
questions.a: PIQs should add new insight — your thinking, motivations and growth — not repeat information readers already have.

weeks.prep: Help the student create (or log into) a StudentAid.gov account. Gather the parents' prior-prior-year federal tax return and the student's (the FAFSA for a school year uses tax information from two years earlier). Parents who are contributors need their own StudentAid.gov accounts. Open the Federal Student Aid Estimator. Note California's priority date (the Cal Grant deadline).
misconceptions: Not filing because 'we make too much.' Many colleges and California programs (including the Middle Class Scholarship and some institutional aid) require the FAFSA or CADAA.
Thinking all aid is free money. Loans must be repaid; grants and scholarships don't.
Missing contributor consent. Each required contributor (e.g. parents of a dependent student) must provide consent and information, or the FAFSA is incomplete.
weeks.assessment_key: FAFSA checklist (pass when complete): StudentAid.gov accounts for student and contributors; FAFSA submitted (or dated practice worksheet) listing every school the student applied to; contributor sections completed with consent; confirmation saved; FAFSA Submission Summary reviewed for errors; California deadline noted. Aid quiz: 1) Cost of attendance = tuition/fees + housing + food + books/supplies + transportation + personal expenses. 2) Grant = need-based, no repayment. 3) Scholarship = merit/other criteria, no repayment. 4) Work-study = part-time job earnings for students with need. 5) Loan = must be repaid with interest. 6) SAI = Student Aid Index, an eligibility number schools use to determine need. 7) Need = COA − SAI (minus other aid). 8) Most undergraduates under 24 are considered dependent students.

days.guide: Break down COA for a UC, a CSU and a community college using each school's published budget.

questions.q: What does cost of attendance include?
questions.a: Tuition and fees, housing, food, books and supplies, transportation and personal expenses.

days.guide: Chart grants, scholarships, work-study and loans: who pays, repaid or not, sources.

questions.q: Which types of aid don't have to be repaid?
questions.a: Grants and scholarships (work-study is earned by working).

days.guide: Create or review StudentAid.gov accounts and run the Federal Student Aid Estimator.

questions.q: What does the Student Aid Index (SAI) do?
questions.a: It's a number from the FAFSA that colleges use to determine how much need-based aid a student is eligible for.

days.guide: Complete or review each FAFSA section, invite contributors and list schools; mark the state priority date.

questions.q: Why list every college you applied to on the FAFSA?
questions.a: Each listed school receives your FAFSA information so it can build an aid offer.

days.guide: Give the aid quiz and verify FAFSA status or the dated practice worksheet.

questions.q: COA is $36,000, SAI is $10,000. What is the financial need?

weeks.prep: Read CSAC's guidance on which application to file (csac.ca.gov). Read the Cal Grant GPA verification rules for private and homeschool students and the WebGrants student portal (mygrantinfo.csac.ca.gov). Prepare the school's GPA certification or check CSAC's current test-score alternative.
misconceptions: Filing both the FAFSA and the CADAA. Students should file only one; filing both can delay or cancel state aid.
Assuming a homeschool GPA reaches CSAC automatically. A private school (PSA) must submit GPAs to CSAC or use the approved alternative — confirm before the deadline.
Ignoring WebGrants messages. Award notices and requests for information appear there.
weeks.assessment_key: State-aid checklist (pass when complete): correct application chosen and submitted (FAFSA for U.S. citizens and eligible noncitizens; CADAA for undocumented students, DACA recipients, students with U visas or TPS, and others eligible for AB 540 benefits); Cal Grant GPA submitted (school certification or approved alternative) by the deadline; WebGrants account created with school list confirmed; reminders set to check monthly; deadlines and confirmation numbers logged.

days.guide: Explain who files the CADAA vs. the FAFSA and why not to file both.

questions.q: Who should file the California Dream Act Application?
questions.a: Students who are undocumented, have DACA, or otherwise can't get federal aid but qualify for California aid (e.g. through AB 540 nonresident tuition exemption eligibility).

questions.q: Should a student file both FAFSA and CADAA?
questions.a: No — file only one; filing both can cause delays or problems with state aid.

days.guide: Walk through CADAA sections and compare to FAFSA.

questions.q: What aid can CADAA filers receive?
questions.a: California state aid such as Cal Grants, the Middle Class Scholarship, the California College Promise Grant and institutional aid — not federal aid.

days.guide: Learn how Cal Grant GPA verification works for a private homeschool and prepare the certification.

questions.q: Why is GPA verification needed for a Cal Grant?
questions.a: Cal Grant awards require a verified GPA meeting the minimum (e.g. 3.0 for Cal Grant A, 2.0 for Cal Grant B) submitted by the deadline.

days.guide: Create a WebGrants account; find award status and messages; set monthly reminders.

questions.q: What is WebGrants used for?
questions.a: CSAC's student portal to check Cal Grant and Middle Class Scholarship status, update schools and respond to requests.

days.guide: Complete the state-aid checklist.

questions.q: What does CSAC stand for?
questions.a: California Student Aid Commission.

weeks.prep: Read csac.ca.gov pages for Cal Grant A, B and C, the Middle Class Scholarship, and the California College Promise Grant; check the current award amounts and income/asset ceilings (they change yearly). Have a calculator.
misconceptions: Thinking Cal Grant B is less valuable. Cal Grant B provides a living-expense 'access award' and, after the first year (in most cases), tuition — often valuable for low-income students.
Forgetting income and asset ceilings. Cal Grants have family income and asset limits along with GPA minimums.
Assuming community college is free automatically. The California College Promise Grant waives the $46-per-unit enrollment fee for eligible students; many colleges also have local promise programs.
weeks.assessment_key: State-aid estimate rubric: 4 = for three schools lists likely Cal Grant type and amount (A: tuition/fees at UC/CSU; B: access award of roughly $1,650 for living costs plus tuition after the first year; C: for career/technical programs), MCS estimate where eligible, CCPG for community college, sources cited and current-year figures used; 3 = minor errors; 2 = missing a program; 1 = incomplete. Eligibility check key: Cal Grant A minimum GPA 3.0; Cal Grant B minimum GPA 2.0; Cal Grant C for occupational/technical programs; all require meeting income/asset ceilings, California residency (or AB 540), and filing by the deadline.

days.guide: Chart Cal Grant A, B and C: what each pays, where, and eligibility.

questions.q: What does Cal Grant A pay for?
questions.a: Tuition and fees at UC and CSU (and part of tuition at eligible private colleges).

questions.q: What minimum GPA does each require?
questions.a: Cal Grant A: 3.0; Cal Grant B: 2.0; Cal Grant C: for career/technical programs (GPA submitted but no set minimum in most cases — check current rules).

days.guide: Determine sample students' eligibility from income, assets, GPA and deadline data.

questions.q: A student has a 2.6 GPA, low income and filed on time. Which Cal Grant might they get?
questions.a: Cal Grant B (GPA ≥ 2.0 but below the 3.0 needed for A).

days.guide: Read the MCS page and estimate an award for a sample UC/CSU student.

questions.q: Who is the Middle Class Scholarship for?
questions.a: UC and CSU undergraduates (and some community college bachelor's programs) whose family income and assets are below the program's ceiling — including many middle-income families that don't qualify for Cal Grants.

days.guide: Research the California College Promise Grant and local free-tuition programs.

questions.q: What does the California College Promise Grant cover?
questions.a: It waives community college enrollment fees ($46 per unit).

days.guide: Build a total state-aid estimate for the top three schools.

questions.q: Why use current-year figures from csac.ca.gov?
questions.a: Award amounts and income ceilings change each year.

weeks.prep: Bookmark scholarship search sites (Fastweb, Bold.org, local community foundations, employers, churches, clubs) and the FTC's scholarship scam page. Set up a tracker (spreadsheet).
misconceptions: Paying for scholarship searches. Legitimate scholarships don't charge fees; 'guaranteed' scholarships are scams.
Skipping small local scholarships. Smaller, local awards have fewer applicants and better odds.
Not reporting outside scholarships. Colleges must be told; award displacement may reduce other aid (ask whether loans or grants are reduced first).
weeks.assessment_key: Scholarship applications rubric: 4 = two complete applications (or fully prepared) meeting all requirements; essay adapted to each prompt with a specific story and clear connection to goals; recommendation and transcript requests sent on time; tracker with 10 scholarships, deadlines, requirements and status; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = only one application or generic essay; 1 = incomplete. Scam quiz: red flags = application or 'processing' fees, guaranteed winnings, requests for bank/credit card numbers, 'you've won' a scholarship you never applied for, high-pressure deadlines.

days.guide: Search local, community, employer and online scholarships; list 10 with deadlines and requirements.

questions.q: Why prioritize local scholarships?
questions.a: Fewer applicants compete, so odds are better.

days.guide: Identify red flags of scholarship scams using FTC guidance.

questions.q: Name two red flags of a scholarship scam.
questions.a: Requiring a fee, guaranteeing you'll win, or asking for bank or credit card information.

days.guide: Draft a 500-word essay adaptable to multiple prompts.

questions.q: How can one essay be reused for different prompts?
questions.a: Keep a strong core story and rewrite the opening and conclusion to answer each prompt directly.

days.guide: Complete and submit (or fully prepare) two applications.

questions.q: What is award displacement?
questions.a: When a college reduces other financial aid because you received an outside scholarship.

days.guide: Revise with parent feedback and log applications in the tracker.

questions.q: What should the tracker include?
questions.a: Name, amount, deadline, requirements, submission date and status.

weeks.prep: Gather three sample aid offers in different formats (NGPF and many colleges post examples) or the student's real offers. Open a spreadsheet, College Scorecard and the StudentAid.gov Loan Simulator. Prepare the Unit 9 test.
misconceptions: Treating loans as part of the 'award'. Some offers list loans alongside grants; subtract only grants and scholarships to find net price.
Comparing only one year. Multiply by four (or the expected years to graduate) and check whether grants are renewable.
Not appealing. Colleges can adjust aid for changed circumstances (job loss, medical costs); a polite, documented appeal can help.
weeks.assessment_key: Unit 9 test answers: 1) COA components. 2) Grants/scholarships vs. loans vs. work-study. 3) SAI meaning; need = COA − SAI. 4) FAFSA vs. CADAA — file only one. 5) Cal Grant A (3.0 GPA, tuition at UC/CSU), B (2.0 GPA, access award + tuition after year one), C (career/technical). 6) Middle Class Scholarship for UC/CSU students under income/asset ceilings. 7) California College Promise Grant waives the $46/unit CCC fee. 8) Scholarship scam red flags. 9) Net price = COA − grants − scholarships; example: COA $34,000, grants $18,000, scholarship $2,000, loans $5,500 → net price $14,000 (loans are a way to pay it, not a reduction). 10) Rule of thumb: total student debt at or below expected first-year salary. Mastery 8+/10. Decision memo rubric: 4 = compares four-year net cost, expected debt and monthly payment vs. starting salary for each option, plus fit factors (program, graduation rate, location), and makes a justified choice; 3 = mostly complete; 2 = cost only or fit only; 1 = incomplete.

days.guide: Label grants, loans and work-study on three offers in different formats.

questions.q: An offer lists a 'Direct Unsubsidized Loan $2,000'. Is that free money?
questions.a: No — it's a loan that must be repaid with interest (and interest accrues while in school).

days.guide: Build a spreadsheet comparing four-year net cost and expected debt across offers.

questions.q: COA $30,000/year; grants $12,000/year; scholarship $1,000/year (renewable). Four-year net price?
questions.a: ($30,000 − $13,000) × 4 = $68,000 (assuming costs stay the same).

days.guide: Compare projected loan payments to starting salaries for the intended major using College Scorecard.

questions.q: $27,000 in loans at 6.39% on a 10-year plan is about $305/month. Is that manageable on a $45,000 salary?
questions.a: Yes by common guidelines — $305 is about 8% of gross monthly income ($3,750), under the 10% rule of thumb, and total debt is below first-year salary.

days.guide: Write a professional financial-aid appeal letter for a sample changed circumstance.

questions.q: What should an aid appeal include?
questions.a: Specific change in circumstances, documentation, the amount of help requested, and a polite, professional tone addressed to the financial aid office.

days.guide: Give the Unit 9 test and have the student write the decision memo.

questions.q: Why compare debt to expected salary?
questions.a: It shows whether loan payments will be affordable after graduation.

weeks.prep: Open the local community college's website and catalog and CCCApply (cccapply.org). Find the college's special admission (dual enrollment) form for high school students and its counseling/orientation pages.
misconceptions: Thinking community college is only for transfer. It also offers career certificates, associate degrees and workforce training.
Skipping counseling. A counselor-built education plan prevents wasted units and keeps students on track for transfer or a credential.
Assuming remedial classes are required. Under AB 705/AB 1705, most students start directly in transfer-level English and math, placed using high school records and guided self-placement.
weeks.assessment_key: Community college education plan rubric: 4 = names one goal (certificate, associate degree or transfer); semester-by-semester courses with units that total the requirement (e.g. 60 semester units for an associate degree); includes orientation, placement, counseling and priority registration steps; notes financial aid (CCPG) and deadlines; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = units don't add up or missing steps; 1 = incomplete.

days.guide: Explore the catalog; list three certificates, three AA/AS degrees and unit requirements.

questions.q: How many semester units is a typical associate degree?
questions.a: 60 semester units (90 quarter units).

questions.q: What's the difference between a certificate and an associate degree?
questions.a: A certificate is a shorter, career-focused program; an associate degree includes general education plus a major, about 60 units.

days.guide: Walk through CCCApply; note residency, education and enrollment questions.

questions.q: Why does CCCApply ask about residency?
questions.a: California residents pay the low resident fee ($46/unit); nonresidents pay much higher tuition unless exempt (e.g. AB 540).

days.guide: Map orientation, placement (guided self-placement), counseling and the education plan.

questions.q: What does AB 705 (and AB 1705) require of community colleges?
questions.a: That students be placed into transfer-level English and math whenever they are likely to succeed, using high school records and guided self-placement rather than placement tests.

days.guide: Research how homeschool students take community college classes now (special admit) and what transfers.

questions.q: How can a homeschool student take community college classes before graduating?
questions.a: Through special admission (dual/concurrent enrollment), usually with a parent/school administrator approval form; units are often limited per term.

days.guide: Create a semester-by-semester community college plan for one goal.

questions.q: What is priority registration?
questions.a: Earlier enrollment for students who complete orientation, assessment/placement and an education plan (and certain groups), so they can get needed classes.

weeks.prep: Open ASSIST.org, the UC Transfer Admission Guarantee (TAG) and UC Transfer Pathways pages, and CSU's Associate Degree for Transfer (ADT) pages. Note: Cal-GETC replaced IGETC and CSU GE-Breadth for students starting community college in fall 2025 or later.
misconceptions: Thinking any 60 units will transfer. Units must be transferable and include major preparation listed on ASSIST.org.
Assuming an ADT guarantees a specific CSU campus. It guarantees admission to the CSU system (not necessarily a particular campus or major) with priority consideration for a similar major.
Missing the TAG filing window. UC TAGs are filed in September of the year before transfer.
weeks.assessment_key: Two-year transfer plan rubric: 4 = names target university and major; 60 transferable units over four semesters including Cal-GETC (34 units) and major preparation from ASSIST.org; TAG or ADT path and deadlines (TAG in September; UC application in the fall; Cal State Apply in the fall); cost comparison of 2 years CCC + 2 years university vs. 4 years at the university with numbers; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = units not transferable or missing major prep; 1 = incomplete.

days.guide: Explain ADT (CSU guarantee) and UC TAG eligibility.

questions.q: What does an Associate Degree for Transfer guarantee?
questions.a: Admission to the CSU system (with priority consideration for a similar major) and that only 60 more units are needed for the bachelor's degree in that major.

questions.q: How many UC campuses offer the Transfer Admission Guarantee?
questions.a: Six: Davis, Irvine, Merced, Riverside, Santa Barbara and Santa Cruz.

days.guide: Use ASSIST.org to find courses at a local CCC that meet major prep for a target UC/CSU major.

questions.q: What is articulation?
questions.a: An agreement showing which courses at one college are accepted as equivalent to courses at another.

days.guide: Map Cal-GETC into a two-year schedule.

questions.q: What is Cal-GETC?
questions.a: The California General Education Transfer Curriculum — a single 34-unit general education pattern accepted by both UC and CSU, starting fall 2025.

days.guide: Build a full 60-unit transfer plan with TAG/ADT deadlines.

questions.q: When is the UC TAG application due?
questions.a: During September (Sept 1–30) of the year before you plan to transfer.

days.guide: Present the plan and compare four-year net cost with the direct freshman path.

questions.q: Two years at a CCC cost $3,000 total in fees and the university costs $15,000/year net. Compare 2+2 vs. four years at the university (fees/tuition only).
questions.a: 2+2: $3,000 + $30,000 = $33,000; four years: $60,000; savings about $27,000 (living costs aside).

weeks.prep: Have a resume template, a real local job posting, and a word processor. Line up a parent/mentor to review and two potential references (former supervisors, coaches, volunteer coordinators — not relatives).
misconceptions: Listing duties instead of accomplishments. Use action verb + task + result/number.
A generic cover letter. Tailor each letter to the posting and include its keywords (applicant tracking systems scan for them).
Fancy formatting that confuses ATS software. Use a simple, clean layout with standard headings.
weeks.assessment_key: Resume and cover letter rubric (4 levels): 4 = one page; contact info; education (homeschool program name, expected graduation, relevant courses/honors); experience and volunteer work with quantified accomplishment statements starting with action verbs; skills and certifications; no errors; cover letter addressed to a person if possible, names the job, connects two or three qualifications to the posting's keywords, ends with a call to action; references confirmed; 3 = minor errors; 2 = duty lists or generic letter; 1 = incomplete.

days.guide: Compare chronological, skills-based and student resume samples; pick a format.

questions.q: Which resume format suits a student with little work history?
questions.a: A student or skills-based (functional/hybrid) resume that highlights education, projects, volunteer work and skills.

days.guide: Rewrite 10 duties into quantified accomplishment statements with action verbs.

questions.q: Rewrite: 'Responsible for helping customers.'
questions.a: 'Assisted 50+ customers per shift, resolving questions quickly and earning a 'staff pick' recognition' (any action verb + task + measurable result).

days.guide: Draft a one-page resume including homeschool education, volunteer work, skills and certifications.

questions.q: How should a homeschool student list education?
questions.a: List the homeschool's name (the private school name on the affidavit) or 'Homeschool', city, expected graduation date, GPA if strong, and notable courses, AP exams or college classes.

days.guide: Write a tailored cover letter for a real local posting, matching keywords.

questions.q: What is an ATS?
questions.a: An applicant tracking system — software that scans and ranks applications, often by keywords from the job posting.

days.guide: Revise after review and request two references.

questions.q: Who makes a good reference?
questions.a: An adult who has supervised or worked with you (employer, coach, volunteer coordinator, teacher) and isn't a relative; ask permission first.

weeks.prep: Download California form B1-1 (Statement of Intent to Employ a Minor and Request for Work Permit) from the CDE website. Find two real job postings. Download Form I-9 and its List of Acceptable Documents, a W-4, and a sample direct-deposit form. Note: students who are 18 or older don't need a work permit.
misconceptions: Thinking homeschoolers can't get work permits. Minors in a private homeschool can get a permit; for a private school, it is typically issued by the local public school district (or the school's authorized administrator, per district practice).
Ignoring minor hour limits. Ages 16–17: during school weeks up to 4 hours on a school day, 8 hours on a non-school day, 28 hours per week; during vacation up to 8 hours a day and 48 hours a week.
Bringing the wrong I-9 documents. Bring one List A document (e.g. U.S. passport) or one List B (e.g. driver's license/state ID) plus one List C (e.g. Social Security card or birth certificate).
weeks.assessment_key: Application packet check (pass when complete): one real or complete practice online application with accurate availability, work history and screening answers; resume attached; B1-1 completed (student, parent and employer sections as applicable) with the correct district identified; I-9 Section 1 practice completed and documents identified; W-4 and direct-deposit form practiced; job tracker entry with date, position, company, contact and follow-up date.

days.guide: Find five local jobs; evaluate pay, schedule and requirements.

questions.q: What should you check in a job posting besides pay?
questions.a: Schedule and hours, location/commute, requirements, age limits, benefits and how to apply.

days.guide: Complete a full online application including availability, work history and screening questions.

questions.q: Why must availability on an application be accurate?
questions.a: Employers schedule based on it; overstating availability leads to conflicts or losing the job.

days.guide: Read California's minor work permit rules and complete form B1-1; learn where to obtain the permit and hour limits.

questions.q: During a school week, how many hours may a 16- or 17-year-old work?
questions.a: Up to 4 hours on a school day, 8 on a non-school day, and 28 hours per week.

questions.q: Which form does the student fill out to request a work permit?
questions.a: Form B1-1, Statement of Intent to Employ a Minor and Request for Work Permit; the issued permit is form B1-4.

days.guide: Practice I-9 documents, W-4 and direct-deposit forms.

questions.q: What does Form I-9 verify?
questions.a: Identity and authorization to work in the United States.

questions.q: Give a valid I-9 document combination.
questions.a: A U.S. passport alone (List A), or a state ID card (List B) plus a Social Security card (List C).

days.guide: Submit one real application (or complete practice packet) and log it.

questions.q: When should you follow up on an application?
questions.a: About one week after applying, with a short, polite email or call.

weeks.prep: Have a phone or webcam for recording and a list of common interview questions. Arrange an adult (ideally not a parent — a family friend or mentor) for a 20-minute mock interview.
misconceptions: Unstructured, rambling answers. Use STAR: Situation, Task, Action, Result.
Not researching the company. Know what it does and why you want to work there.
Forgetting the thank-you. Send a short thank-you email within 24 hours.
weeks.assessment_key: Mock interview rubric (4 levels): 4 = professional greeting and appearance; confident 30-second introduction; answers to behavioral questions use STAR with specific results; shows knowledge of the company; asks two thoughtful questions; good eye contact and pace; thank-you email sent within 24 hours that references something specific from the interview; 3 = solid with a few weak answers; 2 = vague answers, little preparation; 1 = unprepared.

days.guide: Compare phone, video, group and behavioral interviews; research a target company.

questions.q: What is a behavioral interview question?
questions.a: A question about past behavior to predict future performance, e.g. 'Tell me about a time you solved a problem.'

days.guide: Write five STAR stories (teamwork, conflict, failure, leadership, initiative).

questions.q: What does STAR stand for?
questions.a: Situation, Task, Action, Result.

days.guide: Write and record a 30-second elevator pitch; revise.

questions.q: What belongs in a 30-second pitch?
questions.a: Who you are, relevant skills/experience, and what you're looking for or can offer.

days.guide: Run the 20-minute recorded mock interview with 10 common questions.

questions.q: How should you answer 'What's your greatest weakness?'
questions.a: Name a real but manageable weakness and the specific steps you're taking to improve it.

days.guide: Self-score with the rubric and send a professional thank-you email.

questions.q: What should a thank-you email include?
questions.a: Thanks for their time, a specific point from the conversation, a brief restatement of interest, and a professional closing.

weeks.prep: Open the California Labor Commissioner (dir.ca.gov/dlse) and Cal/OSHA pages. Check the current state minimum wage ($16.90/hour in 2026; some cities and industries, such as fast food at $20, are higher). Prepare the Unit 11 test.
misconceptions: Thinking breaks are optional favors. California law requires a 30-minute unpaid meal break for shifts over 5 hours (can be waived by mutual consent if the shift is no more than 6 hours) and a paid 10-minute rest break per 4 hours worked or major fraction.
Fear of retaliation. Retaliating against workers for reporting wage or safety violations is illegal; complaints can be filed with the Labor Commissioner or Cal/OSHA.
Overly casual work emails. Use a clear subject, greeting, short body and professional sign-off.
weeks.assessment_key: Unit 11 test answers: 1) Resume accomplishment statements use action verb + result. 2) ATS definition. 3) STAR method. 4) Minor work permit = B1-1 request, B1-4 permit. 5) I-9 verifies identity and work authorization. 6) California daily overtime after 8 hours. 7) Meal break: 30 minutes for shifts over 5 hours. 8) Rest break: 10 minutes per 4 hours. 9) Paid sick leave: at least 40 hours (5 days) per year. 10) Report wage theft to the Labor Commissioner; unsafe conditions to Cal/OSHA. 11) Comparing offers: total compensation = pay + benefits − commute costs. Mastery 9+/11. Job-offer evaluation example: Job A $18/hour, 30 hrs/week, 20-minute commute; Job B $20/hour, 30 hrs/week, 40-mile round-trip commute at $0.20/mile cost → A = $540/week; B = $600 − (5 days × 40 × $0.20 = $40) = $560/week before time cost.

days.guide: Write three professional emails: requesting time off, following up on an application, asking a supervisor for feedback.

questions.q: What makes an email professional?
questions.a: Clear subject line, proper greeting, concise purpose, polite tone, correct grammar and a signature with your name.

days.guide: Research California minimum wage, overtime, meal and rest breaks and paid sick leave; make a rights card.

questions.q: How much paid sick leave must California employers provide?
questions.a: At least 40 hours or 5 days per year (since 2024).

questions.q: When is a meal break required?
questions.a: For shifts over 5 hours: a 30-minute meal break (waivable by mutual consent if the shift is 6 hours or less).

days.guide: Learn how to report unsafe conditions and harassment; roles of Cal/OSHA and the Labor Commissioner.

questions.q: Where do you report unpaid wages in California?
questions.a: The Labor Commissioner's Office (Division of Labor Standards Enforcement).

questions.q: What should you do first if you experience harassment at work?
questions.a: Document what happened (dates, details, witnesses) and report it to a supervisor or HR per the company's policy; you can also file with the California Civil Rights Department.

days.guide: Evaluate two sample job offers by total compensation, schedule, growth and commute.

questions.q: Why include commute costs in comparing jobs?
questions.a: Gas, transit, parking and time reduce the real value of the pay.

days.guide: Give the Unit 11 test in the key.

questions.q: Is it legal for an employer to fire you for reporting a safety hazard?
questions.a: No — retaliation is illegal; you can file a complaint with the Labor Commissioner or Cal/OSHA.

weeks.prep: Gather the course list from Unit 8, a transcript template and a copy of each year's filed Private School Affidavit (filed with the CDE each October 1–15). Have the school's name and CDS code (if assigned) ready.
misconceptions: Calculating GPA with credits ignored. Weight each grade by its credits if course lengths differ.
Thinking the state issues homeschool diplomas. In a private (PSA) homeschool, the school administrator (usually the parent) issues the diploma.
Losing records. Keep permanent digital and paper copies — colleges, employers and the military may ask years later.
weeks.assessment_key: Signed final transcript and records packet (pass when complete): transcript shows school name, address and affidavit/CDS info; student info; courses by year with a–g letters, grades and credits (10 per year-long course); cumulative GPA (check: sum of grade points × credits ÷ total credits); total credits; graduation date; administrator signature and date; matches the self-reported application records. Records packet contains transcript, course descriptions, reading lists, test scores, work samples and copies of affidavits. GPA example: year grades A, A, B, C, A, B (equal credits) → (4 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 4 + 3) ÷ 6 = 3.33.

days.guide: Calculate cumulative unweighted GPA and total credits.

questions.q: Grades (equal credits): A, B, B, A, C, A, B, A. Unweighted GPA?
Six year-long courses per year for four years at 10 credits each. Total credits?
questions.a: 240 credits.

days.guide: Finalize the transcript: school name, affidavit info, courses by year, a–g letters, grades, GPA, graduation date, signature.

questions.q: Why list a–g letters on the transcript?
questions.a: It helps UC/CSU and counselors quickly see which courses meet a–g subject requirements.

days.guide: Learn that the PSA administrator issues the diploma; review graduation requirements; compare with the CHSPE.

questions.q: What is the CHSPE?
questions.a: The California High School Proficiency Examination; passing it earns a Certificate of Proficiency, legally equivalent to a California high school diploma (eligible at age 16 or after completing 10th grade, among other criteria).

days.guide: Assemble the permanent records packet.

questions.q: Why keep copies of Private School Affidavits?
questions.a: They document that the homeschool was a legally operating private school in California each year.

days.guide: Parent signs and seals the final transcript; the student makes digital and paper copies.

questions.q: What makes a transcript 'official'?
questions.a: It is signed and dated by the school administrator and sent directly (often in a sealed envelope or securely electronically) to the receiving institution.

weeks.prep: Gather the Unit 7 capstone budget, aid or job offers, and a presentation tool. Check deadlines: UC and CSU freshman Statements of Intent to Register are typically due May 1. Invite a guest for the final presentation.
misconceptions: Missing post-acceptance steps. Accepting an offer requires the Statement of Intent to Register (and deposit/waiver), housing applications, orientation and final transcripts.
Forgetting adult obligations. Men must register with Selective Service within 30 days of turning 18; voter registration, health insurance and important documents also need attention.
Treating the budget as finished. Update it with real aid, wages and costs and revisit it every few months.
weeks.assessment_key: Capstone presentation and portfolio rubric (4 levels): 4 = clear launch plan (college/job/gap year) with completed enrollment or acceptance steps and dates; first-year budget updated with actual aid and wages and balanced; adulting checklist complete (voter registration, Selective Service if applicable, health insurance plan, bank accounts, credit freeze, secure copies of birth certificate, Social Security card, ID); digital portfolio with resume, transcript, PIQs, budget and career report; confident 10-minute presentation and thoughtful answers; final reflection names specific growth; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = missing major components; 1 = incomplete.

days.guide: Complete enrollment or job acceptance steps (or a gap-year plan with milestones).

questions.q: What is a Statement of Intent to Register?
questions.a: The UC/CSU form (with deposit or waiver) a student submits to accept an admission offer; typically due May 1 for freshmen.

days.guide: Update the Unit 7 life budget with actual aid, wages and costs.

questions.q: Your aid covers $8,000 of a $12,000 housing cost. How much per month over 9 months must you cover?

days.guide: Complete the adulting checklist.

questions.q: Who must register with Selective Service, and when?
questions.a: Most men ages 18–25 living in the U.S., within 30 days of turning 18.

questions.q: At what age can Californians pre-register to vote?
questions.a: 16 (registration becomes active at 18).

days.guide: Assemble the digital portfolio.

questions.q: What documents belong in the portfolio?
questions.a: Resume, transcript, PIQs, budget and career report (plus work samples).

days.guide: Present the launch plan and portfolio; complete the final reflection.

questions.q: Name one financial habit you'll keep from this course and why.
questions.a: Answers vary; strong answers are specific (e.g. autopay full credit card balance to avoid interest and build credit).

HSS.overview: Semester 1 is American Government and Civics; Semester 2 is Economics. Ground each lesson in a primary source or real data (the Constitution, Supreme Court opinions, the California Voter Guide, FRED, BLS), have the student explain ideas aloud before writing, and connect every topic to California and the student's own community. Expect a short written product most days; use the rubrics and answer keys to grade, and check current figures (minimum wage, district maps, rates) against the official sites since they change.

weeks.prep: Print the Declaration of Independence (archives.gov), short excerpts of Hobbes's Leviathan (ch. 13) and Locke's Second Treatise (chs. 2, 9), Magna Carta clause 39, and the English Bill of Rights (1689). Skim them yourself first.
misconceptions: Thinking Hobbes and Locke agree because both use the 'state of nature.' Hobbes concludes people need an absolute sovereign; Locke concludes government is limited and exists to protect natural rights.
Believing the Declaration created the government. It justified independence; the Articles and later the Constitution created governments.
Assuming the Framers copied Athens. They feared direct democracy and borrowed more from the Roman Republic and English practice.

days.guide: Read the Hobbes and Locke excerpts aloud and make a two-column chart (state of nature, why form government, limits on government). The student writes a comparison paragraph; check that it names each thinker's conclusion.

questions.q: How does Hobbes describe life without government?
questions.a: 'Solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short' — a war of all against all, so people surrender rights to an absolute sovereign for security.

questions.q: Why do people form government according to Locke?
questions.a: To protect natural rights to life, liberty, and property; government rests on consent and can be replaced if it violates those rights.

days.guide: Explain Athenian direct democracy and the Roman Republic's elected representatives, Senate, and checks. The student charts features the Framers adopted or rejected.

questions.q: Which feature of the Roman Republic did the Framers adopt?
questions.a: Representative government (elected officials, a Senate) and a mix of checks among offices.

questions.q: Why did the Framers reject Athenian direct democracy?
questions.a: They feared it was unstable and open to majority passion; it also wasn't practical for a large country.

days.guide: Read Magna Carta clause 39 and the English Bill of Rights. The student highlights limits on the monarch and finds the matching U.S. provisions.

questions.q: What does Magna Carta (1215) clause 39 guarantee?
questions.a: No free man may be imprisoned or punished except by the lawful judgment of his peers or the law of the land — the root of due process.

questions.q: Name two English Bill of Rights provisions that reappear in the U.S. Constitution.
questions.a: No excessive bail or cruel and unusual punishments (8th Amendment); right to petition (1st Amendment); no taxes without Parliament's consent (Congress's power to tax).

days.guide: Read the Declaration's second paragraph aloud and underline Locke's ideas. The student sorts the grievances into categories (taxation, courts, military, self-government).

questions.q: Which Lockean ideas appear in the second paragraph?
questions.a: Unalienable rights (life, liberty, pursuit of happiness), government by consent of the governed, and the right to alter or abolish a destructive government.

questions.q: Give one grievance about taxation and one about the military.
questions.a: 'Imposing Taxes on us without our Consent'; 'keeping among us, in times of peace, Standing Armies without the Consent of our legislatures.'

days.guide: Give the quiz, then the 300-word response. Check that the response uses evidence from at least two documents. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: In what year was the Declaration adopted and who was its principal author?
questions.a: 1776; Thomas Jefferson.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: 1) Hobbes — absolute sovereign for security. 2) Locke — life, liberty, property; consent; right of revolution. 3) Magna Carta 1215, limits king, due process. 4) English Bill of Rights 1689. 5) Declaration 1776, Jefferson. 6) Rome — representative republic. Response rubric (4 = exemplary, 3 = proficient, 2 = developing, 1 = beginning): 4 = clear claim (usually Locke), evidence from the Declaration and one other document, explanation of influence, acknowledges other influences.

weeks.prep: Use the National Constitution Center's Interactive Constitution. Print Federalist 10, 51 (excerpts), 78 (excerpts), Brutus No. 1 (excerpt), and Tocqueville on 'tyranny of the majority.' Prepare the Unit 1 test and DBQ documents.
misconceptions: Reading Madison as anti-faction in the sense of banning parties. He argues you can't remove the causes of faction without destroying liberty, so you control its effects.
Thinking the Anti-Federalists opposed any national government. They feared a distant, consolidated government and demanded a bill of rights.
Confusing separation of powers with checks and balances. Separation divides functions; checks let each branch limit the others.

days.guide: List the Articles' weaknesses together. The student matches each to the Constitution's fix. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Name three weaknesses of the Articles and the Constitution's fix.
questions.a: No power to tax (Congress may tax); no regulation of interstate commerce (Commerce Clause); no national executive or courts (Articles II and III); amendments required unanimity (Article V three-fourths).

days.guide: Read Federalist 10 in chunks. The student explains Madison's argument in steps: definition, causes, cure. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What is a faction and why can't its causes be removed?
questions.a: A group united by an interest adverse to others' rights or the common good; its causes are sown in human nature and liberty, so removing them would destroy liberty.

questions.q: How does a large republic control faction?
questions.a: It includes many interests, making it harder for any one faction to form a majority and oppress others; representatives filter public views.

days.guide: Read 51 and 78 excerpts. The student diagrams checks and balances with an example for each arrow. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Explain 'ambition must be made to counteract ambition.'
questions.a: Each branch is given the means and motive to resist encroachment by the others; 'If men were angels, no government would be necessary.'

questions.q: Why does Hamilton call the judiciary the 'least dangerous' branch?
questions.a: It has 'neither force nor will, but merely judgment' — no army or purse.

days.guide: Read Brutus No. 1 and the Tocqueville excerpt. The student explains how the Bill of Rights answered these fears. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What did Brutus fear?
questions.a: That a large republic couldn't work and the Necessary and Proper and Supremacy Clauses would let the national government swallow the states.

questions.q: What is 'tyranny of the majority'?
questions.a: Tocqueville's warning that a democratic majority can oppress minorities through law and public opinion.

days.guide: Give the Unit 1 test with a DBQ essay on how the Constitution limits government power. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Name three ways the Constitution limits government power.
questions.a: Separation of powers, checks and balances, federalism (also enumerated powers and the Bill of Rights).

weeks.assessment_key: Test key: Articles weaknesses/fixes; Fed 10 faction; Fed 51 checks; Fed 78 judiciary; Brutus fears; Tocqueville. DBQ rubric (4 = exemplary, 3 = proficient, 2 = developing, 1 = beginning): 4 = thesis naming specific limits (separation of powers, checks, federalism, Bill of Rights), uses 4+ documents with accurate interpretation, outside knowledge, explains why limits matter.

weeks.prep: Print the Bill of Rights. Set up iCivics 'Do I Have a Right?' Prepare 10 First Amendment scenarios and a short Kelo v. New London summary (Oyez).
misconceptions: Thinking the First Amendment protects all speech everywhere. It limits government, not private employers, and allows some limits (true threats, incitement, time/place/manner).
Believing the Bill of Rights originally applied to states. It limited only the federal government until incorporation through the 14th Amendment.
Confusing eminent domain with confiscation. The Takings Clause requires public use and just compensation.

days.guide: Read the First Amendment's five freedoms. The student classifies 10 scenarios; check reasoning for each. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Can a public school punish a student for a silent armband protest?
questions.a: Not unless it substantially disrupts school (Tinker v. Des Moines, 1969).

questions.q: Can a city require a permit for a large march?
questions.a: Yes — content-neutral time, place, and manner rules are allowed.

days.guide: The student builds the Amendments 2–8 chart with modern examples. Focus on 4th, 5th, 6th, 8th. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What does the 4th Amendment protect?
questions.a: Against unreasonable searches and seizures; generally requires warrants with probable cause.

questions.q: Name three 5th Amendment protections.
questions.a: Grand jury indictment, no double jeopardy, no self-incrimination, due process, just compensation.

days.guide: Explain the 14th Amendment's due process clause and selective incorporation. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What is incorporation?
questions.a: The process by which the Supreme Court applied most Bill of Rights protections to the states through the 14th Amendment's due process clause, beginning with cases like Gitlow v. New York (1925).

days.guide: Discuss economic rights and Kelo. The student analyzes the ruling and the backlash. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What did Kelo v. New London (2005) decide?
questions.a: 5–4: taking private homes for economic development counts as 'public use' under the Takings Clause; many states then limited eminent domain.

days.guide: Play iCivics; give the quiz. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What does the 9th Amendment say?
questions.a: Listing certain rights doesn't deny others retained by the people.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: 1) Five freedoms: religion, speech, press, assembly, petition. 2) 2nd: bear arms. 3) 3rd: quartering. 4) 4th: search/seizure. 5) 5th: self-incrimination, double jeopardy, due process, takings. 6) 6th: speedy public trial, counsel. 7) 7th: civil jury. 8) 8th: no cruel/unusual punishment, excessive bail. 9) 9th: unenumerated rights. 10) 10th: reserved powers. 11) Incorporation via 14th. 12) Kelo 2005.

weeks.prep: Print or open the USCIS civics test (uscis.gov). Note: the 2008 version has 100 questions; a 2025 revision expanded the bank — use whichever USCIS currently posts. Find California jury information (courts.ca.gov) and sss.gov. Line up an interview with a volunteer or nonprofit leader.
misconceptions: Thinking citizenship only means rights. Discuss obligations: jury service, obeying laws, paying taxes, Selective Service for men 18–25.
Believing civil society means government. Civil society is voluntary associations outside government.
Position essays that ignore the other side. Address the strongest counterargument.

days.guide: The student takes the civics test and researches naturalization requirements. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Name three requirements for naturalization.
questions.a: Usually 18+, lawful permanent resident for 5 years (3 if married to a citizen), good moral character, English and civics tests, oath of allegiance.

days.guide: Research jury duty and Selective Service. The student writes about why each matters. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Who must register with Selective Service?
questions.a: Nearly all men ages 18 through 25 living in the U.S.

questions.q: Name two California juror qualifications.
questions.a: U.S. citizen, 18+, resident of the county, able to understand English.

days.guide: Read Tocqueville on associations. The student maps 10 local civic organizations. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Why did Tocqueville admire American associations?
questions.a: Americans formed voluntary groups to solve problems themselves, building civic skills and checking government.

days.guide: The student interviews a volunteer/nonprofit leader and writes notes. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Give two good interview questions.
questions.a: 'How does your group influence public decisions?' and 'What obstacles do you face?'

days.guide: Give the Unit 2 test and the position essay. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Give a thesis on rights vs. responsibilities.
questions.a: Rights depend on citizens accepting responsibilities like jury service, since rights like a fair trial require them.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 2 test: citizenship requirements, obligations, civil society. Position essay (4 = exemplary, 3 = proficient, 2 = developing, 1 = beginning): 4 = clear thesis, 2+ examples, counterargument.

weeks.prep: Print Article I. Look up your U.S. Representative (house.gov) and Senators (senate.gov) and their committee assignments in advance. Bookmark congress.gov.
misconceptions: Thinking senators represent districts. Each senator represents the whole state; representatives serve districts.
Treating the elastic clause as unlimited. 'Necessary and proper' powers must connect to an enumerated power (McCulloch).
Confusing the Speaker with the Senate's presiding officer. The Vice President presides over the Senate; the majority leader sets its agenda.

days.guide: Read Article I, Sections 1–3. The student charts qualifications, terms, and unique powers of each chamber; quiz orally. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Give the age, citizenship, and term for House and Senate.
questions.a: House: 25, 7 years a citizen, 2-year term. Senate: 30, 9 years a citizen, 6-year term.

questions.q: Name a unique power of each chamber.
questions.a: House: originates revenue bills, impeaches. Senate: tries impeachments, confirms appointments, ratifies treaties (two-thirds).

days.guide: Model looking up a member's committees and votes on congress.gov. The student summarizes all three members. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: How many representatives does California have, and why?
questions.a: 52 (after the 2020 census) — House seats are apportioned by population.

days.guide: Read Article I, Section 8 and sort the powers. Discuss the elastic clause. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Give one power in each category: money, commerce, defense.
questions.a: Tax and borrow/coin money; regulate interstate and foreign commerce; declare war and raise armies.

days.guide: Diagram congressional leadership and committees. Explain standing, select, joint, and conference committees. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Who leads the House?
questions.a: The Speaker, elected by the House majority.

days.guide: Give the Congress quiz. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: How many members are in the House and Senate?

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: 1) House 25/7/2 yrs; Senate 30/9/6 yrs. 2) 435 and 100. 3) House originates revenue bills, impeaches. 4) Senate tries impeachments, confirms, ratifies treaties. 5) Elastic clause = Necessary and Proper. 6) Speaker leads House; VP presides over Senate. 7) California has 52 representatives. 8) Committees do most bill work.

weeks.prep: Print Article V. Bookmark congress.gov bill tracker. Prepare a bill template.
misconceptions: Thinking most bills become law. The large majority die in committee.
Assuming the president can veto parts of a bill. There is no line-item veto for presidents (Clinton v. City of New York, 1998).
Confusing proposal and ratification of amendments.

days.guide: Flowchart the process: introduction, committee, floor, other chamber, conference, president, override. The student explains each step.

questions.q: How can Congress override a veto?
questions.a: Two-thirds vote in both houses.

questions.q: What is a pocket veto?
questions.a: If Congress adjourns within 10 days (excluding Sundays) of sending a bill and the president doesn't sign it, it dies.

days.guide: The student tracks one bill and records sponsor, committee, status. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Where do most bills stall?
questions.a: In committee.

days.guide: Simulate a markup and floor vote. The student writes and defends a short bill. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What happens in markup?
questions.a: The committee debates and amends the bill before voting to report it.

days.guide: Read Article V; compare 19th, 26th, and the ERA. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: How are amendments proposed and ratified?
questions.a: Proposed by two-thirds of both houses (or a convention called by two-thirds of states); ratified by three-fourths of states.

questions.q: What did the 19th and 26th Amendments do?
questions.a: 19th (1920) women's suffrage; 26th (1971) voting age 18.

days.guide: The student writes the 400-word reflection; give the quiz. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Why did the Framers make lawmaking slow?
questions.a: To encourage deliberation and compromise and guard against hasty, factional majorities.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: veto override 2/3; pocket veto; most bills die in committee; amendment process 2/3 + 3/4; ERA failed to reach 38 states. Mock bill rubric (4 = exemplary, 3 = proficient, 2 = developing, 1 = beginning): 4 = clear purpose, sections, amendment record, vote tally, reflection.

weeks.prep: Print Article II. Pick a recent executive order on federalregister.gov. Gather Cuban Missile Crisis documents (DocsTeach, JFK Library). Set up iCivics 'Executive Command.'
misconceptions: Believing executive orders are laws. They direct the executive branch and must rest on the Constitution or a statute; courts can strike them.
Thinking the president can declare war. Only Congress declares war; the president is commander in chief.
Treating the bureaucracy as separate from the president. Departments are part of the executive branch.

days.guide: Read Article II; list formal powers. Discuss informal powers. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Name four formal presidential powers.
questions.a: Commander in chief, make treaties (with Senate consent), appoint officials (with Senate consent), veto, pardon.

questions.q: What is the 'bully pulpit'?
questions.a: Theodore Roosevelt's term for using the presidency's visibility to persuade the public.

days.guide: Read the executive order; identify the legal basis and limits. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Where does an executive order's authority come from?
questions.a: The Constitution (Article II) or powers granted by Congress through statute.

days.guide: Diagram the 15 executive departments; the student researches one independent agency. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Name four executive departments.
questions.a: State, Treasury, Defense, Justice (also Interior, Agriculture, Commerce, Labor, HHS, HUD, Transportation, Energy, Education, Veterans Affairs, Homeland Security).

days.guide: Analyze Cuban Missile Crisis documents; evaluate Kennedy's options. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What options did Kennedy consider and choose?
questions.a: Airstrike, invasion, diplomacy, or a naval blockade; he chose a 'quarantine' (blockade) plus negotiation; the USSR removed missiles and the U.S. pledged not to invade Cuba (and privately agreed to remove missiles from Turkey).

days.guide: Give the quiz and play the game. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: How many executive departments are there?

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: formal powers; executive orders; 15 departments; Cuban Missile Crisis 1962 blockade. Case study (4 = exemplary, 3 = proficient, 2 = developing, 1 = beginning): 4 = options, risks, decision, evaluation with documents.

weeks.prep: Print Article III. Find a short confirmation-hearing clip (C-SPAN). Pick a recent Supreme Court opinion syllabus (supremecourt.gov). Prepare Unit 3 test.
misconceptions: Thinking the Supreme Court hears all appeals. It chooses a small share through certiorari.
Confusing the holding with the reasoning.
Assuming justices serve fixed terms. They serve during 'good behaviour' (life tenure).

days.guide: Diagram the federal courts; locate California in the Ninth Circuit. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: How many levels are in the federal court system?
questions.a: Three: district courts, courts of appeals (13 circuits), Supreme Court.

days.guide: Explain certiorari and the rule of four. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What is the rule of four?
questions.a: Four justices must vote to grant certiorari for the Court to hear a case.

questions.q: About what share of petitions are granted?
questions.a: Around 1% — roughly 60–80 cases from several thousand petitions per year.

days.guide: Watch a hearing segment; evaluate senators' questions. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What is the Senate's role?
questions.a: Advice and consent — confirms nominees by majority vote.

days.guide: Read a syllabus; identify question, holding, reasoning. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What is a 'holding'?
questions.a: The Court's answer to the legal question.

days.guide: Give the Unit 3 test. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Name one check on the judiciary.
questions.a: Senate confirmation, impeachment, constitutional amendments, or Congress setting jurisdiction.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 3 test key: 1) House 25/7/2; Senate 30/9/6. 2) Veto override two-thirds of both houses. 3) Amendment: two-thirds proposal, three-fourths ratification. 4) Commander in chief, treaties, appointments, veto, pardon. 5) Executive orders need constitutional or statutory basis. 6) 15 departments. 7) District courts → 13 courts of appeals → Supreme Court; California in the Ninth Circuit. 8) Rule of four; roughly 1% of petitions granted. 9) Senate confirms justices by majority. 10) One check on each branch. Scoring: 90%+ mastery, 75–89% proficient, 60–74% developing.

weeks.prep: Open Oyez summaries for Marbury v. Madison (1803), McCulloch v. Maryland (1819), and United States v. Nixon (1974). Print short essays on originalism and living constitutionalism (e.g., National Constitution Center).
misconceptions: Thinking judicial review is written in the Constitution. Marshall inferred it in Marbury.
Reading McCulloch as letting Congress do anything. It allows implied powers connected to enumerated ones.
Equating judicial 'activism' with a political side. Both liberal and conservative courts strike down laws.
