days.guide: Read Marshall's key lines ('It is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is'). The student explains the case's logic step by step.

questions.q: What did Marbury v. Madison establish?
questions.a: Judicial review — courts can strike down laws that conflict with the Constitution; part of the Judiciary Act of 1789 was void.

questions.q: Why was the ruling politically clever?
questions.a: Marshall denied Marbury his commission (avoiding a clash with Jefferson) while claiming a major power for the Court.

days.guide: Analyze McCulloch. The student explains both holdings. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What were McCulloch's two holdings?
questions.a: Congress could create a national bank under the Necessary and Proper Clause (implied powers); Maryland could not tax it, because 'the power to tax involves the power to destroy' and federal law is supreme.

days.guide: Listen to Oyez audio excerpts of Nixon. The student explains limits on executive privilege. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What did U.S. v. Nixon decide?
questions.a: Unanimously (8–0), that executive privilege is not absolute; Nixon had to turn over the Watergate tapes. He resigned soon after.

days.guide: Read the philosophy essays; the student applies each to one case. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Define originalism.
questions.a: Interpreting the Constitution according to its original public meaning when adopted.

days.guide: The student writes a 500-word case analysis. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: How did Nixon strengthen checks and balances?
questions.a: It showed no president is above the law and the judiciary can check the executive.

weeks.assessment_key: Case analysis rubric (4 = exemplary, 3 = proficient, 2 = developing, 1 = beginning): 4 = accurate facts, question, holding, reasoning; clear explanation of effect on checks and balances; evidence from the opinion; 500 words.

weeks.prep: Print excerpts of Plessy (with Harlan's dissent), Brown, Tinker, Miranda, Gideon, Bakke. Find a summary of Prop 209 (1996). Prepare moot court roles and Unit 4 test.
misconceptions: Thinking Brown ended segregation immediately. Implementation was slow ('all deliberate speed,' Brown II 1955) and met massive resistance.
Thinking students have no free-speech rights at school or unlimited rights. Tinker protects non-disruptive expression; later cases allow limits.
Confusing civil rights (equal treatment) with civil liberties (freedoms from government).

days.guide: Compare Plessy and Brown, including Harlan's dissent. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What did Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) hold?
questions.a: 'Separate but equal' segregation laws were constitutional.

questions.q: What did Brown (1954) hold and why?
questions.a: Unanimously, that 'separate educational facilities are inherently unequal,' violating equal protection; it cited harm to Black children's sense of status.

questions.q: What did Harlan write?
questions.a: 'Our Constitution is color-blind.'

days.guide: Analyze Tinker and a later case (e.g., Morse v. Frederick or Mahanoy v. B.L.). Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What is the Tinker test?
questions.a: Schools may restrict student speech only if it causes or forecasts substantial disruption or invades others' rights.

questions.q: What did Mahanoy v. B.L. (2021) decide?
questions.a: A school violated a cheerleader's free speech by punishing her off-campus Snapchat post.

days.guide: Analyze Miranda and Gideon. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What does Miranda require?
questions.a: Police must warn suspects in custody of the right to remain silent and to an attorney before interrogation.

questions.q: What did Gideon v. Wainwright (1963) hold?
questions.a: States must provide lawyers to defendants in felony cases who can't afford one.

days.guide: Analyze Bakke and Prop 209. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What did Bakke (1978) decide?
questions.a: Racial quotas in UC Davis medical school admissions were unconstitutional, but race could be one factor.

questions.q: What did Prop 209 do?
questions.a: Banned race and sex preferences in California public education, employment, and contracting (1996).

days.guide: The student argues one side for 5 minutes; take the Unit 4 test. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What makes a strong moot court argument?
questions.a: Clear legal question, precedent, and answers to judges' questions.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 4 test key: 1) Plessy (1896) upheld 'separate but equal'; Harlan: 'Our Constitution is color-blind.' 2) Brown (1954): segregated schools 'inherently unequal,' 14th Amendment equal protection. 3) Tinker (1969): substantial-disruption test. 4) Mahanoy (2021) protected off-campus speech. 5) Miranda (1966): warnings before custodial interrogation. 6) Gideon (1963): right to appointed counsel in state felony cases. 7) Bakke (1978): quotas unconstitutional, race may be one factor. 8) Prop 209 (1996) banned preferences in CA public institutions. Moot court rubric (4 = exemplary … 1 = beginning): 4 = states the legal question, cites the Constitution and 2+ precedents accurately, answers 'bench' questions directly, clear 5-minute delivery.

weeks.prep: Print Washington's Farewell Address excerpt. Bookmark FEC.gov and the Living Room Candidate archive. Find two recent polls with methodology.
misconceptions: Believing the Constitution creates parties. Parties developed despite founders' warnings.
Thinking Citizens United allowed unlimited direct contributions to candidates. It allowed unlimited independent expenditures; direct contributions remain capped.
Treating any poll as accurate. Check sample, margin of error, wording.

days.guide: Read Washington's warning. Trace party systems. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What did Washington warn about?
questions.a: The 'baneful effects of the spirit of party.'

questions.q: Name the first two parties.
questions.a: Federalists (Hamilton) and Democratic-Republicans (Jefferson, Madison).

days.guide: Explain primaries, caucuses, conventions, and California's top-two primary. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: How does California's top-two primary work?
questions.a: All candidates appear on one ballot; the top two vote-getters advance to November regardless of party (Prop 14, 2010).

days.guide: Analyze three campaign ads (e.g., 'Daisy' 1964, 'Morning in America' 1984). Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What technique does 'Daisy' (1964) use?
questions.a: Fear appeal — nuclear war imagery.

days.guide: Use FEC.gov; analyze Citizens United. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What did Citizens United v. FEC (2010) decide?
questions.a: Government can't limit independent political spending by corporations and unions; it led to super PACs.

days.guide: Evaluate two polls; take the quiz. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: A poll shows 48% vs 45% with ±3.5% margin. Is it a clear lead?
questions.a: No — within the margin of error.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) Washington warned of the 'baneful effects of the spirit of party.' 2) First parties: Federalists and Democratic-Republicans. 3) Top-two primary: top two vote-getters advance regardless of party (Prop 14, 2010). 4) Citizens United (2010): no limits on independent expenditures by corporations/unions; direct contributions still capped. 5) 48% vs. 45% with ±3.5% is within the margin of error. Ad analysis rubric (4 levels): 4 = identifies technique (fear, bandwagon, testimonial, etc.), target audience, message, and evaluates effectiveness with historical context for all three ads.

weeks.prep: Visit registertovote.ca.gov. Get a recent Official Voter Information Guide. Explore Citizens Redistricting Commission maps. Prepare Unit 5 test.
misconceptions: Thinking 16-year-olds can vote in California. They can pre-register; registration activates at 18.
Thinking the popular vote elects the president directly.
Confusing gerrymandering with apportionment.

days.guide: Walk through registration. Explain pre-registration. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: At what age can Californians pre-register?
questions.a: 16 or 17; they're automatically registered at 18.

days.guide: Read a proposition in the guide with LAO analysis and pro/con. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What does the LAO provide?
questions.a: Nonpartisan analysis of a measure's fiscal effects.

days.guide: Compare the 2003 and 2021 recalls. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What happened in 2003?
questions.a: Gov. Gray Davis was recalled and Arnold Schwarzenegger elected.

questions.q: What happened in 2021?
questions.a: Gov. Gavin Newsom survived, with about 62% voting no.

days.guide: Explore redistricting maps; explain gerrymandering. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What are 'packing' and 'cracking'?
questions.a: Packing concentrates opposing voters into few districts; cracking splits them across many.

questions.q: Who draws California's districts?
questions.a: The 14-member Citizens Redistricting Commission (Props 11 and 20) draws legislative maps; note that voters approved Prop 50 in 2025 to use legislature-drawn congressional maps temporarily — check current status.

days.guide: Calculate electoral votes and debate; take the Unit 5 test. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: How many electoral votes are there and how many to win?
How many electoral votes does California have (2024–2030)?

weeks.assessment_key: Ballot-measure analysis rubric (4 = exemplary, 3 = proficient, 2 = developing, 1 = beginning): summary, fiscal effect, both arguments, reasoned decision. Unit 5 test: parties, primaries, Citizens United, registration, recall, redistricting, Electoral College.

weeks.prep: Open the California Constitution (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov) and an LAO budget overview. Pick a current California bill to track.
misconceptions: Thinking federal law always wins. Federal law is supreme only within federal powers; states keep reserved powers.
Assuming the California Constitution is like the U.S. one. It is far longer and amended often.
Confusing the Assembly and Senate. The Assembly has 80 members with 2-year terms; the Senate has 40 with 4-year terms — like the U.S. House and Senate.

days.guide: Make a Venn diagram of powers; discuss the 9th and 10th Amendments. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Name a concurrent power.
questions.a: Taxing, borrowing, making courts, enforcing laws.

days.guide: Analyze a federal-state conflict. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What did Gonzales v. Raich (2005) decide?
questions.a: Congress can prohibit homegrown medical marijuana under the Commerce Clause, even where state law allows it.

days.guide: Compare the two constitutions. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: How can the California Constitution be amended?
questions.a: By legislative proposal (two-thirds of each house) or initiative (signatures equal to 8% of the last gubernatorial vote), then majority voter approval.

questions.q: Name a right explicit in California but not the U.S. Constitution.
questions.a: Privacy (Article I, Section 1).

days.guide: Track a bill on leginfo. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: How many members in the Assembly and Senate?

days.guide: Give the federalism quiz. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What does the 10th Amendment reserve?
questions.a: Powers not delegated to the U.S. nor prohibited to states are reserved to the states or the people.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) Federal: coin money, declare war, regulate interstate commerce; state: run elections, set up local governments, regulate intrastate commerce; concurrent: tax, borrow, make courts. 2) 10th Amendment reserves undelegated powers to states or people. 3) Gonzales v. Raich (2005): federal ban on homegrown marijuana upheld under the Commerce Clause. 4) CA amendments: legislature (two-thirds each house) or initiative (8% signatures), then majority vote. 5) Privacy is explicit in CA Const. art. I §1. 6) Assembly 80 members (2-year terms), Senate 40 (4-year terms). Proficient: 5 of 6.

weeks.prep: Get your city/county budget and a council agenda. Visit California Courts website. Research a California tribe's government.
misconceptions: Thinking the city provides everything. Special districts, counties, and school districts provide many services.
Misunderstanding Prop 13 as a cap on all taxes. It limits property tax rates (1%) and assessment increases (2%/yr until sale), which shifted local finance toward other sources.
Thinking tribes are subject to state government like counties. Tribes are sovereign nations with government-to-government relationships.

days.guide: Map who provides water, schools, police, fire, roads, parks. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What is a special district?
questions.a: A local government for one service, like water or fire.

days.guide: Analyze the budget; explain Prop 13. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What did Prop 13 (1978) do?
questions.a: Capped property taxes at 1% of assessed value and limited annual assessment increases to 2% until sale.

days.guide: Research a tribal government. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: About how many federally recognized tribes are in California?
questions.a: More than 100 (about 109).

days.guide: Diagram California courts. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Name the three levels.
questions.a: Superior Courts (58, one per county), Courts of Appeal, Supreme Court (7 justices).

days.guide: Watch a meeting; write summary and public comment; take Unit 6 test. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: How long is a typical public comment?
questions.a: Usually 1–3 minutes.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 6 test key: 1) Special districts provide single services (water, fire). 2) Prop 13 (1978): 1% cap on property tax rate, 2%/yr assessment growth until sale, two-thirds vote for special taxes. 3) Tribes are sovereign with government-to-government relations; CA has about 109 federally recognized tribes. 4) CA courts: 58 superior courts, Courts of Appeal (6 districts), Supreme Court of 7 justices. Meeting report rubric (4 levels): 4 = accurate summary of agenda items and decisions, identifies who decided and how public input was used, a specific 1–3 minute public comment with evidence.

weeks.prep: Find a summary of NYT v. U.S. (1971). Pick a political story covered by three outlets. Gather 5 viral claims to fact-check.
misconceptions: Thinking prior restraint is always banned. It faces a heavy presumption against it.
Assuming any bias means a story is false. Framing shapes emphasis; check facts separately from tone.
Reading vertically (staying on one site) to check credibility. Lateral reading means leaving the site to see what others say about it.

days.guide: Analyze the Pentagon Papers case. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What did NYT v. U.S. hold?
questions.a: 6–3, the government failed to justify prior restraint; the papers could publish.

days.guide: Compare three outlets' coverage. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What is framing?
questions.a: How a story is presented — emphasis, word choice, sources.

days.guide: Practice lateral reading on five claims. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What is lateral reading?
questions.a: Opening new tabs to check what other sources say about a site or claim.

days.guide: Analyze an official's social media and FDR's fireside chats. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What were fireside chats?
questions.a: FDR's radio addresses (1933–1944) speaking directly to Americans.

days.guide: The student writes a media-literacy guide; quiz. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Name three steps to verify a claim.
questions.a: Check the source, read laterally, find the original.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) NYT v. U.S. (1971), 6–3: government failed to justify prior restraint. 2) Prior restraint = government blocking publication in advance. 3) Framing = choices of emphasis, words, and sources. 4) Lateral reading = leaving the site to check what others say about it. 5) FDR's fireside chats were radio addresses. Media-literacy guide rubric (4 levels): 4 = 5+ practical steps with examples (check the source, read laterally, find the original, check date, look for evidence), explains framing and bias vs. accuracy, clear voter audience.

weeks.prep: Print Freedom House reports for two countries. Find Mandela's 1964 Rivonia Trial speech excerpt.
misconceptions: Confusing federal and unitary systems. In a federal system power is constitutionally divided between national and state governments; in a unitary system the national government holds power and can create or abolish local units.
Thinking dictatorships arise only by force. Hitler gained power legally before dismantling democracy.
Treating Freedom House scores as precise facts. They are expert ratings.

days.guide: Compare systems and U.S. vs UK. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: How is the head of government chosen in the UK?
questions.a: The Prime Minister is the leader of the majority in Parliament.

questions.q: Example of a unitary state?
questions.a: France or the UK.

days.guide: Analyze Germany 1933 and Chile 1973. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: How did Hitler consolidate power?
questions.a: Appointed chancellor January 1933; Reichstag fire decree; Enabling Act (March 1933).

questions.q: What happened in Chile in 1973?
questions.a: A military coup led by Pinochet overthrew elected president Allende.

days.guide: Analyze the Mexican Revolution and 1917 constitution. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Whom did the revolution overthrow?
questions.a: Porfirio Díaz.

questions.q: Name two 1917 constitution provisions.
questions.a: Land reform (Article 27) and labor rights (Article 123).

days.guide: Read Mandela's excerpt. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What ideal did Mandela say he was prepared to die for?
questions.a: A democratic and free society with equal opportunities.

days.guide: Write a country comparison; quiz. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What are Freedom House's two categories?
questions.a: Political rights and civil liberties.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) Unitary (UK, France) vs. federal (U.S., Mexico) vs. confederal (Articles of Confederation). 2) Parliamentary PM is chosen by the legislature's majority. 3) Germany 1933: Hitler appointed chancellor, Reichstag fire decree, Enabling Act. 4) Chile 1973: Pinochet's coup overthrew Allende. 5) Mexico: revolution against Díaz (1910); 1917 Constitution — land reform (art. 27), labor rights (art. 123). 6) South Africa's first multiracial election 1994, Mandela president. Comparison rubric (4 levels): 4 = Freedom House scores for political rights and civil liberties, specific evidence for each, explanation of differences.

weeks.prep: Print excerpts of King's 'Letter from Birmingham Jail' (1963; King Institute at Stanford has the text). Help the student brainstorm local or state issues in advance and find the relevant decision-makers (city council, school board, legislators).
misconceptions: Thinking civic action means protest only. Letters, public comment, petitions, testimony, and volunteering are all civic action.
Choosing an issue too big to influence ('end climate change'). Narrow to a local decision with a clear decision-maker.
Not documenting the action. Keep copies, dates, photos, and any replies for the portfolio.

days.guide: Read the excerpts aloud, stopping at the just/unjust law passage. The student lists the tensions King addresses (law vs. justice, order vs. liberty, patience vs. urgency) with a quotation for each.

questions.q: How does King distinguish just from unjust laws?
questions.a: A just law squares with the moral law; an unjust law degrades human personality (e.g., segregation laws). One who breaks an unjust law must do so openly, lovingly, and accept the penalty.

questions.q: Whom does King criticize as a 'great stumbling block'?
questions.a: The 'white moderate' who prefers order to justice and tells activists to wait.

questions.q: Quote King's line about interconnectedness.
questions.a: 'Injustice anywhere is a threat to justice everywhere.'

days.guide: Model researching an issue from three perspectives (e.g., a local housing project). The student chooses an issue, summarizes at least three perspectives with sources, and names who decides.

questions.q: Why identify decision-makers before acting?
questions.a: So the action reaches the people with authority over the decision, making it effective.

days.guide: The student writes a plan: the action, audience, message, timeline, and how they'll document it. Review it for feasibility this week.

questions.q: Name four forms of civic action.
questions.a: A letter to a legislator, public comment at a meeting, a petition, and a volunteer project.

days.guide: The student carries out the action (sends the letter, delivers comment, completes volunteer hours) and documents it. Accompany them to any meeting.

questions.q: What counts as documentation?
questions.a: A copy of the letter or comment, dates, photos or meeting minutes, and any response received.

days.guide: The student writes a reflection on how change happens in a democracy. Discuss it together. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What should the reflection address?
questions.a: What the student did, how decision-makers responded, what they learned about the process, and what they would do next.

weeks.assessment_key: Civic action portfolio rubric (4 = exemplary, 3 = proficient, 2 = developing, 1 = beginning): Research — multiple perspectives with sources; Plan — clear audience, message, timeline; Action — completed and documented; Reflection — thoughtful analysis of how change happens, connected to King or course concepts. Proficient: 3 in each.

weeks.prep: Write a review guide and the Government final: 30 multiple-choice/short-answer items plus a DBQ on an enduring constitutional tension (e.g., liberty vs. security) with 5–6 documents (Federalist 51, Bill of Rights, Tinker, King's Letter, a modern case).
misconceptions: Memorizing case names without holdings. Make cards with name, year, question, holding, significance.
Mixing up branch powers. Sort powers into a three-column chart from memory.
Treating a DBQ as document summary. Each document must be used to support the thesis, with outside knowledge.

days.guide: The student creates a one-page study guide on founding principles and the Bill of Rights. Quiz them orally from it. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Name the five First Amendment freedoms.
questions.a: Religion, speech, press, assembly, petition.

questions.q: Which thinker's ideas appear in the Declaration's second paragraph?
questions.a: John Locke's.

days.guide: The student completes a matching set of powers to branches and cases to holdings. Correct together. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Match: Marbury v. Madison, McCulloch v. Maryland, Gideon v. Wainwright.
questions.a: Judicial review; implied powers and federal supremacy; right to counsel in state felony cases.

days.guide: The student presents the civic action project in 5 minutes. Ask two follow-up questions. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What makes a strong civic action presentation?
questions.a: Clear issue, action taken with evidence, results, and lessons learned.

days.guide: The student retakes the USCIS civics test and completes a practice exam; review misses. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What is the supreme law of the land?
questions.a: The Constitution.

questions.q: How many amendments does the Constitution have?

days.guide: Administer the final with DBQ. Grade with the key. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Give an enduring constitutional tension.
questions.a: Liberty vs. order/security, majority rule vs. minority rights, or federal vs. state power.

weeks.assessment_key: Final exam key: foundations (Locke, Magna Carta, Federalist 10/51/78); Bill of Rights and incorporation; Congress (terms, powers, lawmaking, veto override 2/3); president (powers, executive orders); courts (certiorari, Marbury, McCulloch, Nixon, Brown, Tinker, Miranda, Gideon); elections (top-two, Electoral College 538/270); federalism and California government. DBQ rubric (4 levels): 4 = clear thesis on the tension, uses 4+ documents accurately, outside knowledge, analysis of how the tension has been balanced over time; 3 = solid with 3 documents; 2 = summary; 1 = minimal.

weeks.prep: Graph paper and Khan Academy Microeconomics (Basic economic concepts). Have the student gather a rough weekly schedule and spending list for Day 1.
misconceptions: Thinking opportunity cost is the money spent. It is the value of the next-best alternative given up (including time and forgone income).
Counting sunk costs in decisions. Past, unrecoverable costs shouldn't affect choices at the margin.
Treating points inside the PPF as impossible. Inside = inefficient (unused resources); outside = unattainable.

days.guide: Define scarcity (unlimited wants, limited resources). The student lists 10 scarce resources in their life and the trade-off each forces; check that each names a specific choice.

questions.q: Why is time a scarce resource?
questions.a: Everyone has only 24 hours a day, so every activity means giving up another.

days.guide: Model opportunity cost of college vs. working: tuition and fees plus forgone wages (not room and board, which you'd pay either way). The student computes with real numbers.

questions.q: Four years of wages at $35,000/yr forgone plus $14,000/yr tuition and fees. Opportunity cost?
Why might college still be worth it?
questions.a: Higher lifetime earnings and lower unemployment for degree holders typically exceed the cost, plus nonmonetary benefits.

days.guide: Graph a household PPF (meals vs. cleaning hours). The student labels efficient, inefficient, and unattainable points and explains the bowed shape.

questions.q: Why is a PPF usually bowed outward?
questions.a: Resources aren't equally suited to both tasks, so opportunity cost increases as you specialize more in one.

questions.q: What shifts a PPF outward?
questions.a: More resources, better technology, or improved skills.

days.guide: Build an MB/MC table for pizza slices. The student finds the optimal quantity where MB ≥ MC for the last unit. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: MB of slices: $5, $4, $3, $2, $1; each costs $2.50. How many slices?
questions.a: 3 — the third slice's MB ($3) exceeds $2.50, but the fourth's ($2) does not.

days.guide: Give the fundamentals quiz. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Define marginal analysis.
questions.a: Comparing the additional benefit and additional cost of one more unit of an activity.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: 1) Scarcity = limited resources vs. unlimited wants. 2) Opportunity cost = next-best alternative. 3) College example = $196,000. 4) PPF points: on = efficient, inside = inefficient, outside = unattainable. 5) Bowed shape = increasing opportunity cost. 6) Pizza: 3 slices. 7) Sunk costs ignored. Proficient: 6 of 7.

weeks.prep: Print excerpts from The Wealth of Nations (Book I ch. 1 pin factory; Book IV ch. 2 'invisible hand') and a short Marx excerpt (Communist Manifesto). Find GDP-per-capita data for North/South Korea or East/West Germany (Maddison Project, World Bank).
misconceptions: Equating 'invisible hand' with 'no rules.' Smith assumed laws, property rights, and competition.
Thinking all economies are pure types. Real economies are mixed.
Ignoring nonmonetary incentives.

days.guide: Define incentives. The student classifies 10 and predicts behavior; check predictions are specific. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Is California's bottle deposit (CRV) monetary or nonmonetary? Predicted effect?
questions.a: Monetary — people return more bottles and cans for the refund.

days.guide: Read the pin-factory and invisible-hand excerpts. The student summarizes Smith's argument in three sentences. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What did the pin factory show?
questions.a: Division of labor greatly increases productivity — ten workers specializing made thousands of pins a day.

questions.q: Explain the 'invisible hand.'
questions.a: Individuals pursuing their own gain in competitive markets are led to promote society's interest without intending it.

days.guide: Compare North and South Korea with data. The student graphs GDP per capita over time. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What does the Korea comparison suggest?
questions.a: Similar starting points in the 1950s, but South Korea's market economy grew far richer than North Korea's command economy.

days.guide: Discuss property rights and conservation (groundwater, fishing quotas). Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Why do individual transferable fishing quotas help conservation?
questions.a: They give fishers a property stake in the long-run fishery, reducing the race to overfish.

days.guide: Give the Unit 8 test with an essay comparing systems. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Define a mixed economy.
questions.a: One combining markets with government involvement — like the U.S.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 8 test: scarcity, opportunity cost, PPF, marginal analysis, incentives, Smith, systems. Essay rubric (4 levels): 4 = compares market, command, mixed with real evidence (Korea/Germany), addresses property rights, balanced conclusion.

weeks.prep: Graph paper; have grocery receipts handy. Bookmark the EIA California gasoline price series.
misconceptions: Confusing a change in quantity demanded (movement along the curve, caused by price) with a change in demand (shift, caused by other factors).
Mixing up substitutes and complements. Substitutes: price of one rises, demand for the other rises. Complements: price rises, demand for the other falls.
Thinking elastic means 'stretches a lot in price.' Elasticity measures how much quantity responds to price.

days.guide: Survey 10 people at prices $1–$6. The student graphs the market demand curve by summing quantities. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: State the law of demand.
questions.a: Other things equal, as price rises, quantity demanded falls.

days.guide: Model the five shifters. The student graphs 8 scenarios. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: The price of peanut butter rises. What happens to demand for jelly?
questions.a: Decreases (shifts left) — complements.

questions.q: Coffee prices rise. Demand for tea?
questions.a: Increases (shifts right) — substitutes.

days.guide: Teach the midpoint formula. The student classifies three goods. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Price rises $2 → $3; quantity falls 100 → 60. Elasticity?
Gas $4 → $5, quantity 50 → 48 gallons/month. Elasticity?

days.guide: Analyze EIA price data. Discuss why gasoline demand is inelastic short-run. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Why is short-run gas demand inelastic?
questions.a: Few substitutes; people need to commute and can't quickly change cars or homes.

days.guide: Give the demand quiz. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: If a good is elastic, what happens to total revenue when price rises?
questions.a: Revenue falls.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) Law of demand: price up → quantity demanded down. 2) Shifters: income, tastes, prices of related goods, expectations, number of buyers. 3) Peanut butter price up → jelly demand down (complements); coffee price up → tea demand up (substitutes). 4) $2→$3, 100→60: E = 1.25, elastic. 5) Gas $4→$5, 50→48: E ≈ 0.18, inelastic. 6) For elastic goods a price increase lowers total revenue; for inelastic goods it raises revenue. Proficient: 5 of 6.

weeks.prep: Graph paper; make 20 index cards for a pit market (10 buyer cards with maximum prices, 10 seller cards with minimum costs).
misconceptions: Thinking a rise in price causes supply to increase (shift). Price changes cause movement along the supply curve.
Assuming both price and quantity are always predictable when both curves shift. One is indeterminate.
Calling a surplus a shortage. A price above equilibrium creates a surplus (Qs > Qd); below creates a shortage.

days.guide: Build a lemonade supply schedule and graph; list shifters. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: State the law of supply.
questions.a: As price rises, quantity supplied rises.

questions.q: Name three supply shifters.
questions.a: Input costs, technology, number of sellers.

days.guide: Run the pit market for 3–4 rounds and record prices. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What happens to trade prices over rounds?
questions.a: They converge toward the equilibrium price.

days.guide: Find equilibrium from a schedule. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.a: Equilibrium $3, 30 units. At $2, shortage of 20; at $4, surplus of 20.

days.guide: Analyze 6 double-shift scenarios. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: A drought cuts avocado supply. Effect?
questions.a: Price rises, quantity falls.

questions.q: Supply falls and demand rises at once. Effect?
questions.a: Price rises; quantity indeterminate.

days.guide: Give the quiz. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Define equilibrium.
questions.a: Where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) Law of supply: price up → quantity supplied up. 2) Shifters: input costs, technology, number of sellers, expectations, taxes/subsidies. 3) Equilibrium $3, 30 units. 4) At $2 shortage of 20; at $4 surplus of 20. 5) Drought: supply falls → price up, quantity down. 6) Supply down + demand up: price up, quantity indeterminate. Proficient: 5 of 6.

weeks.prep: Find two short articles on rent control in California (one pro, one con) and a summary of the Costa-Hawkins Rental Housing Act. Print Sherman Antitrust Act Sections 1–2. Read a summary of United States v. Google (2024 search ruling).
misconceptions: Thinking a price ceiling must be above equilibrium to matter. A binding ceiling is set BELOW equilibrium; a binding floor is ABOVE it.
Believing being a monopoly is itself illegal. The Sherman Act targets monopolizing through anticompetitive conduct and agreements that restrain trade.
Ignoring evidence that complicates a model. Minimum-wage research finds mixed effects; teach the student to weigh studies.

days.guide: Draw supply and demand for apartments and add a ceiling below equilibrium; label the shortage. Read the articles and discuss Costa-Hawkins; the student writes the strongest argument on each side.

questions.q: What does a binding rent ceiling cause?
questions.a: A shortage (quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied), plus effects like less maintenance and less new construction.

questions.q: What does Costa-Hawkins (1995) do?
questions.a: Limits local rent control in California: it exempts single-family homes and condos and newer construction, and allows landlords to reset rent to market when a unit becomes vacant (vacancy decontrol).

days.guide: Graph the labor market with a minimum wage above equilibrium and label the surplus. Discuss what the model predicts and what research finds.

questions.q: What does the simple model predict from a binding minimum wage?
questions.a: Quantity of labor supplied exceeds quantity demanded — some unemployment — while employed workers earn more.

questions.q: Why might observed job losses be smaller than predicted?
questions.a: Employers may have wage-setting power (monopsony), turnover costs fall, or prices adjust; studies differ by size of the increase and region.

days.guide: Build a chart of the four market structures (number of firms, product type, barriers, price control) with California examples.

questions.q: Give a California example of each structure.
questions.a: Perfect competition: almond or strawberry farmers (near-competitive); monopolistic competition: restaurants; oligopoly: wireless carriers or gasoline refiners; monopoly: a local water utility.

days.guide: Read Sherman Act Sections 1 and 2. The student summarizes the Google case: market, conduct, ruling. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What do Sections 1 and 2 prohibit?
questions.a: Section 1: contracts or conspiracies in restraint of trade; Section 2: monopolizing or attempting to monopolize.

questions.q: What did the court rule in U.S. v. Google (2024)?
questions.a: That Google illegally maintained its monopoly in general search, partly through payments to be the default search engine on phones and browsers.

days.guide: The student writes a one-page policy brief on rent control or minimum wage; then give a short quiz. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What sections belong in a policy brief?
questions.a: Problem, background, analysis (with a graph), options with trade-offs, and a recommendation.

weeks.assessment_key: Policy brief rubric (4 = exemplary, 3 = proficient, 2 = developing, 1 = beginning): 4 = correct graph of the ceiling/floor with shortage or surplus labeled, evidence from both sides, trade-offs for affected groups, clear recommendation. Quiz: binding ceiling below equilibrium → shortage; floor above → surplus; four market structures; Sherman Act §1/§2; Google ruling.

weeks.prep: Pick a California startup story (company website, news profile). Bookmark Investor.gov and FRED (10-year Treasury yield, DGS10). Find a map of California agriculture and industry. Prepare the Unit 9 test.
misconceptions: Thinking profit is guaranteed for entrepreneurs. Profit is the reward for bearing risk; most startups fail.
Believing stocks and bonds are the same. Stocks are ownership; bonds are loans.
Ignoring location factors like water, ports, and talent clusters.

days.guide: Research a startup's origin. The student identifies the risks taken and the profit incentive. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What role do entrepreneurs play?
questions.a: They combine resources in new ways and bear risk in hope of profit, driving innovation.

days.guide: Model break-even: fixed costs ÷ (price − variable cost per unit). The student writes a one-page lean plan. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Fixed costs $600, price $5, variable cost $2 per unit. Break-even quantity?

days.guide: Explain how banks, stocks, and bonds channel savings to investment. The student tracks a stock and the 10-year Treasury yield for a week.

questions.q: What is the difference between a stock and a bond?
questions.a: A stock is partial ownership in a company; a bond is a loan to a company or government that pays interest.

questions.q: If bond prices fall, what happens to yields?
questions.a: Yields rise — they move in opposite directions.

days.guide: Analyze location: Central Valley almonds, Silicon Valley tech, Inland Empire logistics. The student writes one paragraph each.

questions.q: Why is the Inland Empire a logistics hub?
questions.a: Proximity to the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach, available land for warehouses, and highway/rail connections.

days.guide: Give the Unit 9 test. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What is the profit incentive?
questions.a: The expectation of profit that motivates people to start and expand businesses.

weeks.assessment_key: Business plan rubric (4 levels): 4 = clear product and customer, cost table (fixed and variable), price, correct break-even calculation, risks. Unit 9 test: demand/supply shifts, elasticity, equilibrium, price controls, market structures, entrepreneurship, financial markets.

weeks.prep: Print a CARB cap-and-trade overview and the FTC consumer-protection page. Find a short article on California housing permitting delays.
misconceptions: Thinking public goods are anything government provides. A public good is nonexcludable and nonrival.
Believing externalities are always bad. Positive externalities exist (education, vaccines).
Assuming regulation always helps. Compare its costs (compliance, delays) with benefits (cleaner air, safety).

days.guide: Define the four types of goods by excludability and rivalry. The student classifies 10 goods and explains the free-rider problem.

questions.q: Classify national defense, a fishery, streaming service, and a sandwich.
questions.a: Public good; common resource; club good; private good.

questions.q: What is the free-rider problem?
questions.a: People can benefit from a public good without paying, so markets underprovide it.

days.guide: Graph a negative externality with private supply below social cost. Discuss cap-and-trade. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Why does pollution cause overproduction?
questions.a: Producers don't pay the external cost, so market output exceeds the socially optimal level.

questions.q: How does cap-and-trade work?
questions.a: The state caps total emissions and issues tradable allowances; firms that cut cheaply sell extra allowances, putting a price on carbon.

days.guide: Read about the FTC and the CCPA. The student explains the market problem each addresses. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What market problem does consumer protection address?
questions.a: Information asymmetry — sellers know more than buyers.

days.guide: Analyze a case where regulation costs may exceed benefits. The student proposes improvements. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: How can permitting delays raise housing costs?
questions.a: They increase time and uncertainty costs, reducing supply and raising prices.

days.guide: Give the government-role quiz. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Give an example of a positive externality.
questions.a: Education or vaccination benefits others besides the person who receives it.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) Defense = public good; fishery = common resource; streaming = club good; sandwich = private. 2) Free rider benefits without paying → underprovision. 3) Negative externality: social cost above private supply, market overproduces. 4) Cap-and-trade sets an emissions cap with tradable allowances. 5) Consumer protection addresses information asymmetry. 6) Regulation is justified when benefits exceed costs. Proficient: 5 of 6.

weeks.prep: Open CBO budget infographics (cbo.gov) and the California budget summary (ebudget.ca.gov). Bookmark FRED series GFDEGDQ188S (federal debt as % of GDP). Find a federal budget simulator (e.g., CRFB 'Debt Fixer').
misconceptions: Confusing deficit and debt. Deficit is one year's shortfall; debt is the accumulated total.
Thinking foreign aid is a large share of federal spending. It's about 1%.
Calling sales taxes progressive. They take a larger share of income from lower earners (regressive).

days.guide: Analyze CBO charts. The student lists the largest revenue and spending categories. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What are the largest federal spending categories?
questions.a: Social Security, Medicare and other health programs, defense, and net interest.

questions.q: Largest federal revenue source?
questions.a: Individual income taxes, followed by payroll taxes.

days.guide: Compare California's budget sources and spending. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What is California's largest general-fund revenue source?
questions.a: The personal income tax.

questions.q: Largest spending area?
questions.a: K–12 education (guaranteed by Prop 98), followed by health and human services.

days.guide: Compute taxes for incomes $20,000, $50,000, $200,000 under three systems. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Under a 10% flat tax, what does each pay?
Under 0% up to $20,000, 10% to $50,000, 20% above, what does $200,000 pay?

days.guide: Graph debt-to-GDP since 1940. Explain major increases. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: When did debt-to-GDP peak and why?
questions.a: Right after World War II (about 106–119% depending on measure); it rose again after 2008 and 2020.

days.guide: Complete the simulation; give the Unit 10 test. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Give two ways to reduce a deficit.
questions.a: Raise revenue (taxes) or cut spending.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 10 test key: 1) Largest federal spending: Social Security, health (Medicare/Medicaid), defense, net interest. 2) Largest revenue: individual income tax, then payroll taxes. 3) CA: personal income tax; K–12 largest spending (Prop 98). 4) Flat 10%: $2,000/$5,000/$20,000. 5) Progressive example: $200,000 pays $33,000. 6) Deficit = annual shortfall; debt = accumulated. 7) Debt-to-GDP peaked after WWII. Budget simulation rubric (4 levels): 4 = meets the target, explains trade-offs for each choice and who is affected.

weeks.prep: Bookmark the BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook and the BLS chart 'Education pays.' Find California EDD long-term occupational projections for your region. Pick one current article on AI and work.
misconceptions: Thinking wages are set by fairness or effort alone. Wages reflect the supply of and demand for particular skills.
Assuming education guarantees high income. It raises median earnings and lowers unemployment on average.
Believing automation eliminates jobs overall. It shifts demand among tasks and skills.

days.guide: Graph labor supply and demand for two occupations (e.g., surgeons and cashiers). The student explains the wage difference.

questions.q: Why do surgeons earn more than cashiers?
questions.a: High demand for scarce, highly trained skills; long training limits supply.

days.guide: Graph BLS median weekly earnings and unemployment by education. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What does the BLS 'Education pays' data show?
questions.a: Median earnings rise and unemployment falls with each level of education; bachelor's holders earn roughly 1.6–1.7 times high-school graduates' median weekly earnings.

days.guide: The student researches two careers: duties, education, median pay, outlook, regional projections. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What four facts should career research record?
questions.a: Duties, required education, median pay, and job outlook.

days.guide: Read the AI article; discuss which tasks are most and least exposed. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Which skills tend to be complements to automation?
questions.a: Complex problem-solving, interpersonal and creative skills, and skilled trades requiring physical dexterity in varied settings.

days.guide: Give the labor market quiz. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What is human capital?
questions.a: Skills, knowledge, and experience that increase a worker's productivity.

weeks.assessment_key: Career chart rubric (4 levels): 4 = two careers with duties, education, median pay, outlook, regional projection, sources. Quiz: labor supply/demand, human capital, education pays, automation.

weeks.prep: Find a Cesar Chavez speech (UFW website; e.g., his 1984 Commonwealth Club address) and the California Department of Industrial Relations minimum wage page. Prepare union and employer role cards. Prepare Unit 11 test.
misconceptions: Crediting the UFW alone for the Delano grape strike. Filipino workers of the AWOC led by Larry Itliong started it in 1965; Chavez's NFWA joined, and they merged into the UFW.
Thinking minimum wage is uniform. California's is higher than the federal $7.25, and some cities and industries are higher still.
Assuming globalization only hurts workers. It can displace some workers while lowering prices and creating export jobs; discuss both.

days.guide: Read about the AFL, CIO, and UFW; analyze a Chavez speech. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: How did the AFL and CIO differ?
questions.a: AFL organized skilled craft workers; CIO organized whole industries. They merged in 1955.

questions.q: What tactics did the UFW use?
questions.a: Strikes, a national grape boycott, marches, and Chavez's fasts; it led to California's 1975 Agricultural Labor Relations Act.

days.guide: Simulate a contract negotiation. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What is collective bargaining?
questions.a: Negotiation between a union and employer over wages, hours, and conditions.

days.guide: Compare California and federal minimum wages; evaluate research. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What is the federal minimum wage?
questions.a: $7.25 per hour (since 2009).

questions.q: What is California's statewide minimum wage?
questions.a: $16.90 per hour in 2026 (it was $16.50 in 2025); it adjusts yearly for inflation — confirm on the DIR site.

days.guide: Analyze capital mobility and immigration effects. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: How do consumers benefit from offshoring?
questions.a: Lower prices on goods.

days.guide: Give the Unit 11 test. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Who co-founded the UFW with Chavez?
questions.a: Dolores Huerta.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 11 test key: 1) Wages = labor supply and demand. 2) Human capital raises productivity and pay. 3) AFL (crafts) and CIO (industries) merged 1955. 4) Delano grape strike 1965 (AWOC with Itliong; NFWA with Chavez and Huerta) → UFW; 1975 ALRA. 5) Collective bargaining definition. 6) Federal minimum $7.25; California $16.90 (2026). 7) Offshoring lowers consumer prices but can displace workers. Scoring: 90%+ mastery, 75–89% proficient.

weeks.prep: Bookmark FRED series GDPC1 (real GDP) and the latest BEA 'Gross Domestic Product' news release (bea.gov). Prepare 10 transactions to classify.
misconceptions: Counting intermediate goods (flour sold to a bakery) and the final good (bread) — double counting. GDP counts only final goods and services.
Counting transfer payments, used goods, or stock purchases. These don't represent new production.
Comparing nominal GDP across years without adjusting for inflation. Use real GDP for growth.

days.guide: Explain GDP = C + I + G + NX with an example of each. The student classifies 10 transactions as counted (and which component) or not counted; check reasons.

questions.q: Is a used car sale counted? A Social Security check?
questions.a: Neither — the car was counted when new; Social Security is a transfer payment, not payment for production.

questions.q: A California winery exports wine to Japan. Which component?
questions.a: Net exports (exports add to GDP).

days.guide: Teach real GDP = nominal GDP ÷ (price index/100). The student converts and computes growth rates. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Nominal GDP $24 trillion, GDP deflator 120. Real GDP?
questions.a: $24T ÷ 1.20 = $20 trillion (in base-year dollars).

questions.q: Real GDP grows from $20.0T to $20.6T. Growth rate?

days.guide: Graph real GDP since 2000 on FRED with recession shading. The student labels expansions and the 2001, 2008, 2020 recessions.

questions.q: Give the dates of the Great Recession and the COVID recession.
questions.a: December 2007–June 2009; February–April 2020.

questions.q: What is the common rule of thumb for a recession and who officially dates them?
questions.a: Two consecutive quarters of falling real GDP is a rule of thumb; the NBER's Business Cycle Dating Committee officially dates recessions.

days.guide: Read the BEA release headline and summary paragraph together. The student summarizes the growth rate and which components drove it.

questions.q: Which GDP component is largest?
questions.a: Personal consumption expenditures — about two-thirds of U.S. GDP.

days.guide: Give the GDP quiz. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Define GDP.
questions.a: The market value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a given period.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: 1) GDP definition. 2) C + I + G + NX. 3) Not counted: used goods, transfers, intermediate goods, stocks, household work. 4) Real GDP = $20T. 5) Growth 3%. 6) Recessions 2001, 2007–09, 2020. 7) Consumption ≈ 2/3. Proficient: 6 of 7.

weeks.prep: Bookmark the BLS Employment Situation summary and CPI Inflation Calculator, and FRED series CPIAUCSL. Help the student choose 10 basket items they buy regularly and find last year's prices (old receipts or the BLS average-price data).
misconceptions: Counting discouraged workers as unemployed. Unemployed means without work AND actively looking in the past 4 weeks; discouraged workers are out of the labor force.
Confusing the inflation rate with the price level. Falling inflation means prices rise more slowly, not that they fall.
Thinking zero unemployment is achievable or desirable. Some frictional and structural unemployment always exists.

days.guide: Define labor force, unemployment rate, and LFPR, and the three types of unemployment. The student calculates rates from sample data and classifies examples.

questions.q: Employed 155M, unemployed 6M, civilian population 16+ 250M. Unemployment rate and LFPR?
questions.a: Labor force 161M; unemployment 6/161 ≈ 3.7%; LFPR 161/250 = 64.4%.

questions.q: Classify: a graduate searching for a first job; a worker replaced by automation; a worker laid off in a recession.
questions.a: Frictional; structural; cyclical.

days.guide: Read the latest Employment Situation summary together. The student records payroll job change and the unemployment rate and compares with last month.

questions.q: What two headline numbers lead the jobs report?
questions.a: The change in nonfarm payroll employment and the unemployment rate.

days.guide: Price the basket now and a year ago. The student computes their personal inflation rate and compares it with official CPI.

questions.q: Basket costs $200 a year ago and $208 now. Inflation rate?

days.guide: Graph CPI inflation (percent change from a year ago) since 1970. The student annotates the 1970s, 2008–09, and 2021–23. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What caused high inflation in the 1970s?
questions.a: Oil price shocks (1973, 1979) and loose monetary policy; it peaked around 13–14% in 1979–80 until the Volcker Fed raised rates.

questions.q: What was the recent inflation peak?
questions.a: About 9.1% year-over-year in June 2022, driven by pandemic supply disruptions, strong demand, and energy prices.

days.guide: Give the quiz on unemployment and inflation. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Who is hurt most by unexpected inflation?
questions.a: People on fixed incomes and lenders/savers whose interest doesn't keep up; borrowers with fixed-rate loans benefit.

weeks.assessment_key: Personal CPI rubric (4 levels): 4 = 10 items with sources, correct calculation, comparison to official CPI with explanation of differences. Quiz: rates 3.7% and 64.4%; three types of unemployment; CPI 4%; 1970s and 2022 inflation; who's hurt by inflation.

weeks.prep: Read the latest FOMC statement (federalreserve.gov). Bookmark FRED DGS3MO and DGS10 (or T10Y3M). Prepare 10 policy scenarios and the Unit 12 test.
misconceptions: Thinking the Fed prints money to pay government bills. The Fed conducts monetary policy independently; Congress and the president handle fiscal policy.
Confusing fiscal (taxes/spending) and monetary (interest rates/money supply) policy.
Thinking banks lend out deposits only once. Lending creates new deposits throughout the system.

days.guide: Teach money's functions: medium of exchange, store of value, unit of account. Model fractional reserve lending with a T-account.

questions.q: $1,000 is deposited; the reserve requirement is 10%. What is the maximum total new money the system can create?
questions.a: Money multiplier 1/0.10 = 10, so up to $10,000 in total deposits — $9,000 of new money from loans.

days.guide: Read the FOMC statement. The student identifies the decision and reasons. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What is the Fed's dual mandate?
questions.a: Maximum employment and stable prices (about 2% inflation).

days.guide: Graph 3-month vs. 10-year yields. Explain the yield curve. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What is an inverted yield curve and why does it matter?
questions.a: Short-term yields exceed long-term yields; it has preceded most recent U.S. recessions.

days.guide: The student matches 10 scenarios to fiscal or monetary responses and explains trade-offs. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Recession with high unemployment: give one fiscal and one monetary response.
questions.a: Fiscal: cut taxes or raise spending; monetary: lower the federal funds rate.

questions.q: Inflation is 6%: what would the Fed do?
questions.a: Raise interest rates to slow borrowing and spending.

days.guide: Give the Unit 12 test. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Name the Fed's main policy rate.
questions.a: The federal funds rate.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 12 test key: GDP and components; unemployment types and rate; CPI and inflation; money's functions; multiplier; dual mandate; fiscal vs. monetary tools; yield curve. Scoring: 90%+ mastery, 75–89% proficient.

weeks.prep: Find Census trade data for California (census.gov/foreign-trade/statistics/state) and Port of Los Angeles/Long Beach statistics. Graph paper.
misconceptions: Confusing absolute and comparative advantage. Comparative advantage depends on lower opportunity cost.
Thinking trade is zero-sum. Show with the PPF example that both countries can consume more after specializing.
Assuming trade benefits everyone equally. Overall gains can coexist with losses for workers in import-competing industries.

days.guide: Model opportunity costs for two countries. Country A: 6 wheat or 3 cloth per worker; Country B: 2 wheat or 2 cloth. The student determines specialization.

questions.q: Which country has comparative advantage in cloth?
questions.a: B: 1 cloth costs B 1 wheat but costs A 2 wheat.

questions.q: Who specializes in wheat?
questions.a: A — its wheat opportunity cost is 0.5 cloth vs. B's 1 cloth.

days.guide: Graph PPFs and show consumption beyond the PPF after trade. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Give a mutually beneficial terms of trade.
questions.a: Between 1 and 2 wheat per cloth, e.g., 1.5 wheat per cloth.

days.guide: Analyze California's top exports, imports, partners. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Name two of California's top trading partners.
questions.a: Mexico and China (also Canada, Japan, South Korea).

days.guide: Trace trade with Mexico and Canada over the 20th century. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: When did NAFTA take effect?

days.guide: Give the comparative advantage quiz. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Can a country with no absolute advantage still gain from trade?
questions.a: Yes — it still has comparative advantage in something.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) A: 6 wheat or 3 cloth; B: 2 wheat or 2 cloth. A's cost of 1 cloth = 2 wheat; B's = 1 wheat. 2) B specializes in cloth, A in wheat. 3) Terms of trade between 1 and 2 wheat per cloth (e.g., 1.5). 4) Trade lets both consume beyond their PPFs. 5) Top CA partners: Mexico, China, Canada (also Japan, South Korea). 6) NAFTA 1994; USMCA 2020. Proficient: 5 of 6.

weeks.prep: Print the 1930 economists' statement against Smoot-Hawley and a USMCA summary (ustr.gov). Find a current tariff debate article.
misconceptions: Thinking foreign countries pay tariffs. Importers pay them, and costs are usually passed largely to consumers.
Blaming the Depression on Smoot-Hawley alone. It worsened the collapse in trade but didn't cause the Depression.
Ignoring the winners from protection. Protected domestic producers and their workers gain; consumers and import-using industries lose.

days.guide: Read the economists' petition. Discuss effects. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What did over 1,000 economists warn in 1930?
questions.a: That higher tariffs would raise prices, invite retaliation, and hurt exports and farmers.

questions.q: What happened to world trade?
questions.a: It fell sharply in the early 1930s as other countries retaliated.

days.guide: Graph a tariff: world price $10, tariff $2. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What happens to domestic price, production, imports?
questions.a: Price rises to $12; domestic production rises; consumption falls; imports fall; government collects revenue; deadweight loss appears.

days.guide: Evaluate NAFTA and USMCA. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Name one USMCA change.
questions.a: Higher auto rules of origin (75% North American content) and labor value content requirements.

days.guide: Analyze a current debate. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What argument do domestic producers make?
questions.a: Tariffs protect jobs from unfair competition.

days.guide: Hold the debate and write a reflection. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What makes a strong rebuttal?
questions.a: Directly addressing opposing evidence.

weeks.assessment_key: Debate rubric (4 = exemplary … 1 = beginning): Position — clear claim on free trade vs. protection; Evidence — uses Smoot-Hawley history (economists' warning, retaliation, trade collapse), the tariff graph (higher price, fewer imports, deadweight loss, revenue), and NAFTA/USMCA winners and losers; Rebuttal — answers the other side's strongest point; Reflection — explains whether and why their view changed.

weeks.prep: Look up current exchange rates on a currency converter (rates below are illustrative). Bookmark FRED series DTWEXBGS (nominal broad trade-weighted dollar index). Find a news story about a foreign-owned auto or battery plant in California or the U.S. Prepare the Unit 13 test.
misconceptions: Thinking a 'strong dollar' is always good. It helps importers and Americans traveling abroad but hurts exporters and U.S. firms competing with imports.
Confusing appreciation and depreciation. If $1 buys MORE euros than before, the dollar appreciated.
Ignoring capital flows. Exchange rates respond to interest rates and investment demand, not only trade.

days.guide: Convert a $1,000 travel budget at illustrative rates. Explain that exchange rates are set by supply and demand for currencies, influenced by interest rates, inflation, trade, and investor confidence.

questions.q: At 1 USD = 0.90 EUR, 150 JPY, and 18 MXN, what does $1,000 buy?
questions.a: 900 euros, 150,000 yen, and 18,000 pesos.

questions.q: If the rate changes to 1 USD = 0.95 EUR, did the dollar appreciate or depreciate?
questions.a: Appreciate — each dollar buys more euros.

days.guide: Make a two-column chart of winners and losers when the dollar appreciates vs. depreciates. The student fills it in with California examples.

questions.q: Who benefits when the dollar appreciates?
questions.a: U.S. importers, consumers buying imports, and Americans traveling abroad.

questions.q: Who benefits when it depreciates?
questions.a: U.S. exporters (e.g., California almond growers) and the U.S. tourism industry, since foreign buyers find U.S. goods cheaper.

days.guide: Graph the trade-weighted dollar index for 10 years on FRED. The student annotates two big moves with likely causes. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Why might the dollar rise when the Fed raises interest rates?
questions.a: Higher U.S. returns attract foreign investors, increasing demand for dollars.

days.guide: Read the FDI story. The student summarizes the investment, jobs created, and any concerns. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What is foreign direct investment?
questions.a: A foreign company building or buying productive facilities (factories, businesses) in another country, as opposed to buying stocks or bonds.

days.guide: Give the Unit 13 test. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: If the dollar depreciates, what tends to happen to U.S. exports?
questions.a: They rise, because U.S. goods become cheaper for foreign buyers.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 13 test key: 1) Comparative advantage from an opportunity-cost table. 2) Terms of trade between the two opportunity costs. 3) Tariff effects: price up, imports down, deadweight loss. 4) Smoot-Hawley 1930 and retaliation. 5) NAFTA 1994 → USMCA 2020 (auto rules of origin). 6) $1,000 → 900 EUR at 0.90. 7) Appreciation helps importers/hurts exporters. 8) FDI definition. Scoring: 90%+ mastery, 75–89% proficient, 60–74% developing.

weeks.prep: Browse the Legislative Analyst's Office (lao.ca.gov) and CBO (cbo.gov) for reports on housing, minimum wage, gas tax, or tariffs. Bookmark FRED and BLS. Arrange an audience for Day 5.
misconceptions: Choosing a policy too broad ('fix the economy'). Pick one specific policy with an LAO or CBO analysis.
Graphs that shift the wrong curve. A tax on sellers shifts supply left; a subsidy to buyers shifts demand right.
Recommendations without trade-offs. Name who gains and who loses.

days.guide: The student chooses a policy and reads an LAO or CBO analysis, taking notes on goals, costs, and predicted effects. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Why use LAO or CBO reports?
questions.a: They are nonpartisan analyses of fiscal and economic effects, written for lawmakers.

days.guide: Model the supply-and-demand graph for one policy. The student graphs their policy and predicts effects on price, quantity, and different groups.

questions.q: Graph a per-gallon gas tax. What happens?
questions.a: Supply shifts left (or a wedge appears); price paid by consumers rises, price received by sellers falls, quantity falls; the government collects revenue; the burden falls more on consumers because demand is inelastic.

days.guide: The student gathers at least two FRED or BLS data series and makes graphs with sources. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Why use at least two data series?
questions.a: To corroborate the analysis and show the problem from more than one angle.

days.guide: The student writes the 1,000-word analysis: background, model, data, effects on groups, recommendation, trade-offs. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What should the recommendation section include?
questions.a: A clear recommendation, the evidence for it, and an honest statement of who bears the costs.

days.guide: The student presents for 7 minutes and answers questions. Before moving on, have the student answer the check question below without notes, then compare with the answer and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: What three visuals belong in the presentation?
questions.a: The supply-and-demand graph, a data graph, and a summary of the recommendation and trade-offs.

weeks.assessment_key: Policy analysis rubric (4 = exemplary, 3 = proficient, 2 = developing, 1 = beginning): Economic reasoning — correct graph and predictions; Evidence — LAO/CBO source plus two data series cited; Trade-offs — effects on at least three groups; Recommendation — clear and justified; Presentation — 7 minutes, clear visuals, answers questions. Proficient: 3 in each.

weeks.prep: Write three review sets (micro, macro, trade) and the Economics final (about 40 items plus a graph-based short essay). Use AP Macro/Micro free-response questions (College Board, free) for practice.
misconceptions: Mixing up micro and macro tools. Micro studies individual markets; macro studies the whole economy (GDP, inflation, unemployment, policy).
Shifting the wrong curve. Ask: does this change buyers' willingness (demand) or sellers' costs (supply)?
Reversing exchange-rate effects. Re-derive: a stronger dollar makes U.S. exports more expensive abroad.

days.guide: The student completes the micro review; check graphs immediately. Before moving on, have the student answer the check questions below without notes, then compare with the answers and reteach anything missed.

questions.q: Demand for electric cars rises while battery costs fall. Effect on price and quantity?
