questions.a: Multiple copies could be made cheaply and distributed widely — Posada's broadsides reached ordinary people with news and satire.

questions.q: What is ukiyo-e?
questions.a: 'Pictures of the floating world' — Japanese woodblock prints (17th–19th centuries) of landscapes, actors, and daily life.

days.guide: Design the block; reverse the image (trace and flip).

questions.q: How do you prepare a design with text for a relief print?
questions.a: Draw or transfer it mirror-reversed onto the block so it prints correctly.

days.guide: Carve safely; pull test proofs.

questions.q: In relief printing, which areas print?
questions.a: The raised (uncarved) surfaces; carved-away areas stay the paper color.

days.guide: Print an edition of five with consistent registration.

questions.q: What is registration?
questions.a: Aligning the block and paper in the same position for each print (and for multiple colors).

days.guide: Sign and number prints in pencil: edition number (e.g., 3/5) lower left, title center, signature lower right.

questions.q: What does '3/5' on a print mean?
questions.a: It is the third print of an edition of five.

weeks.assessment_key: Print edition rubric. 4 – Five consistent prints with even inking and clean registration, design connects to inquiry, correct reversal, proper signing/numbering, safe carving. 3 (proficient) – Five prints mostly consistent, signed and numbered correctly. 2 – Inconsistent or unsigned. 1 – Fewer than three prints.

weeks.prep: Cardboard, wire, air-dry clay, found objects, hot glue (low-temp, supervise), paint. Images of Betye Saar's The Liberation of Aunt Jemima (1972) and Louise Nevelson's black wood wall assemblages.
misconceptions: Building without an armature, so pieces sag or collapse.
Designing only from the front. Sculpture in the round must work from all sides.
Found objects chosen only for looks; their history adds meaning.

days.guide: Study Saar (reclaimed a racist stereotype image, arming the Aunt Jemima figure to transform its meaning) and Nevelson (unified found wood scraps by painting them one color, usually black).

questions.q: How does Betye Saar's The Liberation of Aunt Jemima transform its found image?
questions.a: She placed a racist mammy figure holding a broom alongside a rifle and pistol with a raised Black Power fist, turning a stereotype into a symbol of resistance.

questions.q: Why did Louise Nevelson paint her assemblages a single color?
questions.a: To unify varied found wood pieces into one composition, emphasizing shape, shadow, and rhythm over the objects' original identities.

days.guide: Build a small maquette.

questions.q: What is a maquette?
questions.a: A small preliminary model of a sculpture.

days.guide: Build the sculpture with armature or assemblage.

questions.q: What is an armature?
questions.a: An internal support framework (wire, wood, foil) that holds the sculpture's form.

days.guide: Finish surfaces; paint or patina.

questions.q: What does 'in the round' mean?
questions.a: Sculpture meant to be viewed from all sides.

days.guide: Photograph from four angles.

questions.q: Why photograph sculpture from multiple angles?
questions.a: A single view can't show the full three-dimensional form.

weeks.assessment_key: Sculpture or assemblage rubric. 4 – Strong 3-D composition from all angles, stable construction, meaningful found objects or forms tied to inquiry, finished surfaces, four quality photos. 3 (proficient) – Stable, finished sculpture with clear intent and documentation. 2 – Unstable or unfinished. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Photos of a local site (park wall, library, underpass — public view, safe access), sketchbook, graph paper for a scaled rendering. Read about Judy Baca's The Great Wall of Los Angeles (begun 1976 in the Tujunga Wash flood-control channel; about 2,754 feet long; painted with hundreds of young people through SPARC; depicts California history from an ethnically diverse perspective).
misconceptions: Designing for yourself rather than the site's community.
Ignoring practical constraints (weather, maintenance, permits, budget).
Thinking public art is only murals. It includes sculpture, installation, and temporary works.

days.guide: Study The Great Wall of Los Angeles and its community process.

questions.q: What made The Great Wall of Los Angeles a community project?
questions.a: Judy Baca worked with hundreds of youth from diverse backgrounds and consulted historians and community members to depict histories often left out of textbooks.

days.guide: Photograph and analyze a site: audience, traffic, history, light.

questions.q: What does 'site-specific' mean?
questions.a: Art created for a particular location, responding to its physical, social, or historical context.

days.guide: Design a mural or installation with a scaled rendering (e.g., 1 inch = 2 feet).

questions.q: A wall is 30 ft × 10 ft. At 1 inch = 2 ft, how big is the rendering?
questions.a: 15 inches × 5 inches.

days.guide: Write a proposal with budget, materials, and community benefit.

questions.q: Name three budget items for a mural.
questions.a: Exterior paint and primer, anti-graffiti/UV clear coat, scaffolding or lifts, brushes/rollers, permits, insurance, artist fees.

days.guide: Present as if to a city arts commission.

questions.q: What do arts commissions usually look for?
questions.a: Artistic quality, community relevance and input, feasibility, safety, durability, and budget.

weeks.assessment_key: Public art proposal rubric. 4 – Site analysis with photos, scaled rendering, design responsive to community and history, realistic itemized budget and timeline, maintenance plan, persuasive presentation. 3 (proficient) – Site analysis, rendering, budget, community benefit, clear presentation. 2 – Missing budget or site response. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Phone or camera on a tripod (or stack of books), two identical lamps (same bulb type) at 45° or indirect window light, neutral gray/white backdrop, gray card or white paper for white balance, editing app.
misconceptions: Shooting at an angle, causing keystoning. Keep the camera centered and parallel to the artwork.
Using mixed light sources (lamp + window), which causes color casts.
Over-editing color so the photo no longer matches the work.

days.guide: Set up two lamps at 45° on either side, equal distance, neutral backdrop.

questions.q: Why place lights at 45° on both sides?
questions.a: It gives even illumination and reduces glare and hot spots.

days.guide: Photograph 2-D works square to the camera; correct glare (adjust angle/polarizer) and keystoning.

questions.q: What is keystoning?
questions.a: Distortion where a rectangle appears as a trapezoid because the camera isn't parallel to the artwork.

days.guide: Photograph 3-D works: multiple views plus a detail.

questions.q: What views should a 3-D work have?
questions.a: Front, side(s), back or three-quarter, and a detail.

days.guide: Crop, color-correct (white balance), export at 1200–2000 px on the long side.

questions.q: What does white balance correct?
questions.a: Color casts from the light source so whites appear neutral.

days.guide: Create an organized archive: title, media, dimensions (H × W × D), date.

questions.q: What order are dimensions listed in?
questions.a: Height × width × depth.

weeks.assessment_key: Digital archive rubric. 4 – All works photographed square, evenly lit, color-accurate, cropped, consistent sizes; 3-D works with multiple views; organized folders with complete metadata (title, media, H × W × D, year). 3 (proficient) – Accurate photos and complete metadata. 2 – Glare, keystoning, or missing info. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Digital archive, printed thumbnails. Check requirements of target colleges (many use SlideRoom; typically 10–20 pieces). Look up National Portfolio Day dates.
misconceptions: Including every piece. Curate: fewer strong works beat many uneven ones.
Ignoring each school's specific requirements.
Random sequencing. Open and close with strong pieces and create visual flow.

days.guide: Write selection criteria for a college portfolio and for an exhibition.

questions.q: How might criteria differ for college admission vs. an exhibition?
questions.a: College: show range of skills, observational drawing, and creative thinking. Exhibition: a cohesive theme and visual impact for the public.

days.guide: Select 15–20 for a college portfolio and 5 for AP-style Selected Works.

questions.q: What does AP Selected Works demonstrate?
questions.a: Five works showing skillful synthesis of materials, processes, and ideas.

days.guide: Sequence with printed thumbnails; justify order.

questions.q: Where should your strongest piece go?
questions.a: First (to make a strong impression), with another strong piece last.

days.guide: Get feedback from a teacher, artist, or National Portfolio Day reviewer.

questions.q: What is National Portfolio Day?
questions.a: Events where representatives from art colleges review prospective students' portfolios and give feedback.

days.guide: Revise selection.

questions.q: What is curation?
questions.a: Selecting and arranging works to communicate ideas and quality.

weeks.assessment_key: Curated portfolio selection rubric. 4 – Written criteria, 15–20 pieces showing range and quality, 5 Selected Works, thoughtful sequence with rationale, revisions documented from outside feedback. 3 (proficient) – Selection, sequence with justification, feedback applied. 2 – Uncurated. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Free portfolio site (Google Sites, Adobe Portfolio, Cargo). Final images and captions. Parental note: use a professional email and avoid posting home address or personal details.
misconceptions: Statements full of jargon ('juxtaposes liminal dichotomies'). Use clear, specific language.
Writing about technique only. Include ideas and why the work matters.
Publishing without testing on a phone.

days.guide: Draft a 200-word statement: inquiry, process, why it matters.

questions.q: What three things should an artist statement address?
questions.a: What you make (subject/media), how you make it (process), and why (ideas and meaning).

days.guide: Revise; remove jargon; read aloud.

questions.q: Why read a statement aloud?
questions.a: To catch awkward phrasing and ensure it sounds like you.

days.guide: Write captions: title, media, size, year, short note.

questions.q: Write a correct caption format.
questions.a: Example: Kitchen Memory, 2025. Graphite and gel transfer on wood, 18 × 24 in. — Note: recipe cards from my grandmother.

days.guide: Build site: gallery, statement, contact.

questions.q: What is a CV for an artist?
questions.a: A list of exhibitions, education, awards, and publications.

days.guide: Publish; test on phone and computer.

questions.q: Why test on mobile?
questions.a: Many viewers, including admissions readers, view portfolios on phones; layouts and image sizes must work.

weeks.assessment_key: Artist statement and published portfolio rubric. 4 – Clear, jargon-free 200-word statement addressing what/how/why; complete captions; site with organized gallery, statement, bio, safe contact info; tested on two devices. 3 (proficient) – Statement, captions, and functioning site. 2 – Unclear statement or missing captions. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Contact potential venues (library community room, co-op, café, church hall) early; floor plan of the venue; label paper; flyer software.
misconceptions: Waiting too long to book a venue.
Hanging work at random heights. Center artworks around 57–60 inches from the floor (museum standard).
Labels missing information.

days.guide: Secure venue and date.

questions.q: What questions should you ask a venue?
questions.a: Dates/hours, wall hanging methods allowed, lighting, insurance/liability, cost, setup times, accessibility.

days.guide: Choose an exhibition title and theme.

questions.q: Why does an exhibition title matter?
questions.a: It frames how visitors understand the work and draws interest.

days.guide: Draw an installation plan placing each work.

questions.q: At what height are artworks typically centered?
questions.a: About 57–60 inches from the floor to the center of the work.

days.guide: Write and print wall labels and an intro panel.

questions.q: What goes on a wall label?
questions.a: Artist name, title (italic), year, medium, dimensions, and optionally a short description or price.

days.guide: Design and send flyer/invitations.

questions.q: What must an invitation include?
questions.a: Title, artist, venue address, dates, opening reception time, and contact/RSVP info.

weeks.assessment_key: Exhibition plan rubric. 4 – Confirmed venue and date, meaningful title and theme statement, scaled installation plan with heights and spacing, complete labels and intro panel, professional flyer distributed. 3 (proficient) – Venue, plan, labels, flyer. 2 – Missing plan or labels. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Acid-free mat board (pre-cut mats are fine), mat cutter if available, acid-free hinging tape, frames, D-rings and hanging wire, screwdriver, level, pedestals or boxes painted white for 3-D work.
misconceptions: Using masking tape or regular tape on artwork. It yellows and damages paper; use acid-free hinging tape.
Hanging work in direct sunlight. UV light fades media.
Using sawtooth hangers on heavy frames. Use D-rings and wire.

days.guide: Research archival practices: acid- and lignin-free materials, UV-filtering glazing, stable humidity (~40–50%), avoid direct sun.

questions.q: Why use acid-free materials?
questions.a: Acidic paper and board yellow and become brittle over time, damaging the artwork they touch.

days.guide: Mat and/or frame 2-D works (hinge at the top with a T-hinge).

questions.q: How should artwork be attached to a mat?
questions.a: With acid-free hinges (e.g., T-hinges) at the top so the paper hangs freely and can expand/contract.

days.guide: Attach hanging hardware; prepare pedestals.

questions.q: Where should D-rings go on a frame?
questions.a: About one-quarter to one-third down from the top on each side, with wire strung between them.

days.guide: Mock hang at home; check spacing and sightlines.

questions.q: Why do a mock hang?
questions.a: To test spacing, order, and visual flow before installation day.

days.guide: Complete exhibition checklist and transport plan.

questions.q: How should framed work be transported?
questions.a: Wrapped with corner protectors and padding, glass taped or protected, stored upright and secured.

weeks.assessment_key: Prepared works rubric. 4 – All works matted/framed or mounted with archival materials, secure hardware, pedestals ready, mock hang photographed, complete checklist and transport plan. 3 (proficient) – Works prepared safely with hardware and checklist. 2 – Some works unprepared or non-archival methods. 1 – Not ready.

weeks.prep: Artwork, labels, level, measuring tape, hooks/nails, guest book, simple refreshments, lighting (clip lights if needed).
misconceptions: Installing without measuring, leading to uneven heights.
Artist talks that read the statement word for word.
Ignoring visitor feedback afterward.

days.guide: Install: measure, level, light, place labels.

questions.q: How do you hang a work centered at 58 inches?
questions.a: Measure 58 in. to the center, add half the frame height, subtract the distance from the hanging wire (pulled taut) to the frame top; place the nail there.

days.guide: Prepare a 5-minute artist talk: inquiry, process, highlights, what's next.

questions.q: What makes a good artist talk?
questions.a: A clear story of the inquiry, specific process moments, connection to viewers, and openness to questions.

days.guide: Host the opening; give the talk.

questions.q: What is a reception?
questions.a: A social event (often the opening) where visitors meet the artist and view the show.

days.guide: Review guest-book comments and conversations.

questions.q: Why review audience feedback?
questions.a: It shows how the work communicates to the public and informs future work.

days.guide: Deinstall carefully; write an exhibition report.

questions.q: What should an exhibition report include?
questions.a: Attendance, what went well, problems and solutions, feedback, photos, lessons for next time.

weeks.assessment_key: Exhibition and artist talk rubric. 4 – Professional installation (level, consistent heights, lighting, labels), engaging 5-minute talk, gracious hosting, thorough report with feedback analysis, careful deinstall. 3 (proficient) – Clean installation, clear talk, report. 2 – Installation issues or weak talk. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Baseline self-portrait from Week 1, mirror, same pencils and lighting. Arrange a mentor conversation (art teacher, local artist).
misconceptions: Growth analysis that only says 'I got better.' Cite specific visual evidence.
Judging only technique. Also assess ideas and process.
Comparing to others rather than to your past work.

days.guide: 45-minute self-portrait under similar conditions; compare with Week 1.

questions.q: Why use the same conditions?
questions.a: So differences reflect growth in skill, not changes in setup.

days.guide: Growth analysis with specific evidence.

questions.q: Give an example of specific evidence of growth.
questions.a: 'In September my shadows were outlined; now the core shadow and reflected light model the cheek.'

days.guide: Evaluate the investigation with technical and conceptual criteria.

questions.q: What is the difference between technical and conceptual criteria?
questions.a: Technical: skill with materials (drawing, value, color, craft). Conceptual: strength and development of ideas and meaning.

days.guide: Discuss the year with a mentor.

questions.q: What questions might you ask a mentor?
questions.a: What's the strongest work and why? What should I develop next? How did you build your practice?

days.guide: Final reflection on artistic identity.

questions.q: What is metacognition?
questions.a: Thinking about your own thinking and learning processes.

weeks.assessment_key: Growth analysis rubric. 4 – Side-by-side self-portraits, specific visual evidence of growth in at least four areas, evaluation through technical and conceptual lenses, mentor insights, thoughtful identity reflection. 3 (proficient) – Comparison with specific evidence and both lenses. 2 – General statements. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Internet access; local community college catalog; list of local open studios or life-drawing groups. Portfolio for the conference.
misconceptions: Thinking art careers mean only fine artist. Many paths use art skills (design, illustration, therapy, conservation, teaching).
Stopping art after high school without a plan.
Summer plans without goals or schedules.

days.guide: Research five careers and pathways.

questions.q: What training does an art therapist need?
questions.a: Typically a master's degree in art therapy plus supervised clinical hours and credentialing (e.g., ATR through the Art Therapy Credentials Board).

questions.q: What does a conservator do?
questions.a: Examines, preserves, and restores artworks using scientific and art-historical knowledge; usually requires a graduate degree.

days.guide: Find local open studios, life-drawing groups, or community-college classes.

questions.q: Why join a community art group?
questions.a: Regular practice, feedback, models/resources, and connection with other artists.

days.guide: Plan a summer project with goals and schedule.

questions.q: What makes a summer art plan realistic?
questions.a: Specific goals, weekly schedule, materials budget, and a finish date.

days.guide: Create a final sketchbook spread summarizing the year.

questions.q: What could a summary spread include?
questions.a: Key images, inquiry question, quotes from reflections, and goals.

days.guide: Portfolio conference: present final portfolio and plan.

questions.q: What is an artist residency?
questions.a: A program providing artists time, space, and sometimes funding to create work, often away from home.

weeks.assessment_key: Final portfolio conference rubric. 4 – Polished portfolio (online and physical), confident presentation of inquiry and growth, researched career/education plan, community resources, specific summer project. 3 (proficient) – Complete portfolio and clear plan. 2 – Incomplete materials or vague plan. 1 – Not prepared.
